about.title: How the Kannada script works
about.text:
Kannada is written left to right in units called aksharas. An akshara is not a single letter of the English kind: it is a whole syllable - a vowel on its own, or a consonant together with the vowel that follows it.

Every consonant letter already contains the short vowel 'a'. So ಕ is not 'k' but 'ka', and ಮ is 'ma'. To get any other vowel you attach a vowel sign to the consonant (ಕಿ ki, ಕು ku). To get a bare consonant with no vowel you add the 'killer' stroke on top (ಕ್ k).

The good news for an English speaker: Kannada is read exactly as it is written. The built-in 'a' is always pronounced, even at the end of a word - ಮರ is ma-ra, never 'mar' - and there are no silent letters. (This is different from Hindi, where the final 'a' is dropped.) Once you know the letters you can read any word aloud correctly.

examples.english: tree (ma + ra: both built-in vowels are spoken)
bus (the stroke on the last letter removes its vowel)

about.title: Vowels: independent letters and vowel signs
about.text:
Each vowel has two shapes. The independent letter (ಅ ಆ ಇ ಈ ...) is used only when the vowel begins a word or syllable on its own. After a consonant the same vowel is written as a sign attached to the consonant. The set of one consonant with every vowel sign is called the kaagunita, and children learn it by chanting: ka, kaa, ki, kee, ku, koo ...

The sign for short 'a' is nothing at all - a plain consonant already has it. Most signs change the top or the right-hand side of the letter. Notice that the ordinary top stroke of the consonant (the 'talekattu') disappears when the signs for i, ee, e and the killer stroke are added: ಕ becomes ಕಿ, ಕೆ, ಕ್.

The long signs for ee, e and o are made by adding the lengthening mark ೕ to the short sign: ಕಿ ki / ಕೀ kee, ಕೆ ke / ಕೇ ke (long), ಕೊ ko / ಕೋ ko (long). Spotting that extra mark is how you tell short from long when reading.

examples.english: mouse (independent i, then l with the i sign)
leg (k + aa sign, l + u sign)

about.title: Short and long vowels change the meaning
about.text:
Kannada has five pairs of short and long vowels: a/aa, i/ee, u/oo, and also short and long e and short and long o. A long vowel is simply held about twice as long as the short one; its quality does not change. Length is not a detail - it makes different words.

The pair that surprises English speakers is e and o. Hindi and Sanskrit have only the long ones, but Kannada has both: ಎ is the short e of 'get', ಏ is the long e, like the vowel of 'gate' said without gliding. ಒ is a short o, ಓ a long 'oh' without the glide.

In this course's romanisation aa, ee and oo show the long a, i and u. Short and long e and o are both written simply as e and o (this keeps the spelling easy to read and matches what the lessons have always used), so for these two vowels trust the Kannada spelling and the notes: whenever a common word has a long e or o that you might get wrong, the note says so.

examples.english: horn (long o) - same romanisation, different word

about.title: Double and joined consonants: the ottakshara
about.text:
When two consonants come together with no vowel between them, the first is written normally and the second is written as a small form underneath or to the lower right of it. This small form is called an ottakshara (or 'ottu'). Most ottaksharas are just a miniature of the letter without its top stroke: ಕ್ಕ kka, ಗ್ಗ gga, ಲ್ಲ lla. A few have their own shape and must be learned: ತ (as in ತ್ತ tta), ನ (ನ್ನ nna), ಮ (ಮ್ಮ mma), ಯ (ಕ್ಯ kya), ರ (ಕ್ರ kra) and ಲ (ಕ್ಲ kla).

A vowel sign is attached to the big letter on top, but it is pronounced after the whole cluster. In ಸ್ನೇಹಿತ (snehita, friend) the e sign sits on ಸ, yet you say s-n-e.

Doubled consonants are extremely common in Kannada and must really be held longer, as in English 'bookkeeper' or 'unnamed'. Doubling changes the meaning, so do not skim over it.

A few clusters have special names and sounds: ಕ್ಷ (ksha) and ಜ್ಞ (written j + ny, pronounced 'gnya' or 'jnya'; romanised jna here).

examples.english: ten (double t; the small lower t has its own shape)
rail track (single l - a different word)
friend (s + n joined; the long e is said after the n)

about.title: The letter ra in clusters: arkavattu
about.text:
The consonant ರ (ra) behaves in two ways in a cluster.

When r comes second (kra, pra, tra) it is written as an ordinary ottakshara, a small hook under the first letter: ಪ್ರ pra, ತ್ರ tra.

When r comes first (rka, rya, rtha) Kannada normally does the opposite of what you expect: the following consonant is written full size, and the r is written after it as a separate sign that looks rather like the numeral ೯. This sign is called the arkavattu. So in ಸೂರ್ಯ you see soo + ya + the r-sign, but you read soo-r-ya: the r is pronounced before the consonant it follows on the page.

This is purely a spelling convention; the sound is a normal r.

examples.english: sun (r is written after the y but spoken before it)
question (here r comes second: an ordinary ottakshara)

about.title: Aspirated, dental and retroflex consonants
about.text:
The 25 main consonants are arranged in five rows by where the tongue touches: k-row (back of the mouth), ch-row (palate), retroflex t-row, dental t-row and p-row (lips). Each row has: plain, aspirated, voiced, voiced aspirated, nasal.

Aspirated letters (ಖ kha, ಘ gha, ಛ chha, ಥ tha, ಧ dha, ಫ pha, ಭ bha ...) are said with a puff of breath. They occur mostly in words borrowed from Sanskrit; in everyday speech many speakers pronounce them almost like the plain letters, but they must be spelled correctly. Note that 'th' in this course is never the English th of 'think': it is t plus breath.

Dental versus retroflex is the distinction that matters most. For the dentals ತ ದ ನ the tip of the tongue touches the back of the upper teeth (softer than English t, d). For the retroflexes ಟ ಡ ಣ the tongue tip curls back and strikes the roof of the mouth (English t and d sound retroflex to Kannada ears, which is why 'doctor' is written ಡಾಕ್ಟರ್). Kannada also has a retroflex l, ಳ, made with the tongue curled back, beside the ordinary ಲ.

The romanisation in this course does not mark the difference (both ತ and ಟ are t, both ದ and ಡ are d, both ನ and ಣ are n, both ಲ and ಳ are l), so learn each word's spelling from the Kannada. Minimal pairs below show why it matters.

ಫ is 'pha' in Sanskrit words but is used for the English f sound in loanwords, where this course writes f (ಕಾಫಿ kaafi, ಫೋನ್ fon).

about.title: Anusvara and visarga
about.text:
The small circle ಂ written after a letter is the anusvara (called 'sonne', which also means zero). It stands for a nasal sound whose exact value depends on the consonant that follows: it becomes the nasal made in the same place as that consonant.

Before k, g it sounds like ng (ಅಂಗಡಿ an-ga-di, as in 'finger'). Before ch, j, t, d (dental or retroflex) it is n (ಸಂಜೆ sanje, ಗಂಟೆ gante, ಬಂದೆ bande). Before p, b it is m (ತುಂಬಾ tumbaa). Before s, sh, h and at the end of a word it is m (ಮಾಂಸ maamsa). The romanisation writes n or m accordingly.

Kannada prefers the anusvara to a written nasal conjunct, so you write ಬಂದೆ rather than ಬನ್ದೆ. But a doubled nasal is written as a real double letter, never with the circle: ಅಮ್ಮ, ಕನ್ನಡ, ಅಣ್ಣ.

The two small circles ಃ are the visarga, a light breathy 'h' that echoes the vowel before it. It appears only in a few Sanskrit words such as ದುಃಖ (sorrow) and ಬಹುಶಃ (perhaps).

examples.english: hour, o'clock, bell (retroflex n before retroflex t)

about.title: Spoken and written Kannada
about.text:
Kannada has a formal written style (used in books, newspapers, news broadcasts and speeches) and an everyday spoken style, and they differ noticeably, mainly in verb endings. Nobody chats in the written style.

This course teaches the standard spoken Kannada of Bengaluru and Mysuru, and the main phrase is always in the spoken form. Where the written form is noticeably different, it is given in the note or in the unit guide, so that you can also recognise it when you read.

The main differences: (1) the present tense is shortened - written maaduttene, spoken maadteeni (I do); (2) person endings differ a little - written -ene, -eve, -eeri; spoken -eeni, -eevi, -eera; (3) in the past tense a short vowel is dropped before the endings -ru, -ri, -lu - written bandaru, spoken bandru (they came); (4) 'it does' is written maaduttade, spoken maadutte; (5) 'not' forms are shortened - written maaduvudilla, spoken maadalla.

One convention in this course: forms built on the infinitive, such as hogabeku (must go), barabahudu (may come) and baralilla (did not come), are written in full. In fast speech their middle 'a' is often dropped too (hogbeku, barlilla); both are understood everywhere.

Spoken forms have no single official spelling, so you will see small variations in messages and film subtitles (for example ಮಾಡ್ತೀನಿ and ಮಾಡ್ತೇನೆ). The spellings used here are the common ones.

examples.english: I do / I will do - spoken
I do / I will do - written
does not / will not come - spoken
does not / will not come - written

about.title: How Kannada words are built: endings and sandhi
about.text:
Kannada is an agglutinating language: instead of separate little words like 'to', 'in', 'from', 'my', 'not' and 'can', it adds endings to the noun or verb, one after another. mane is 'house'; manege is 'to the house'; maneyalli is 'in the house'; maneyallide is 'it is in the house'.

When an ending is attached, the sounds at the join adjust. This is called sandhi. The three everyday patterns are: a final u drops before a vowel (hesaru + enu = hesarenu, 'what name?'); a linking y appears after i and e (mane + alli = maneyalli); a linking v, d, n or in appears after a and u depending on the type of noun (mara + alli = maradalli, huduga + ige = huduganige, ooru + alli = oorinalli). The units on case endings teach these one at a time.

Short common words also fuse with the verb: elli + ide = ellide (where is it?), chennaagi + ide = chennaagide (it is good), hege + iddeera = hegiddeera (how are you?). When a long word puzzles you, look for a familiar word at its beginning and peel the endings off from the right.

examples.english: to the town (ooru + ige; the u drops)

about.title: Romanisation key used in this course
about.text:
The romanisation is a pronunciation aid, always in lower case. Read every letter; nothing is silent.

Vowels: a as in 'about' (short), aa as in 'father', i as in 'bit', ee as in 'feet', u as in 'put', oo as in 'food', e as in 'get' (short) or the 'a' of 'gate' without the glide (long), o short or long 'oh' without the glide, ai as in 'my', au as in 'now', ru for the vowel ಋ.

Not marked: the length of e and o; dental versus retroflex (t, d, n, l each stand for two letters). The Kannada spelling shows these, and the notes point out the cases that matter.

Consonants: ch is always as in 'church'; chh is the same with breath. g is always hard as in 'go'. A consonant followed by h (kh, gh, th, dh, ph, bh, jh) is that consonant plus a puff of breath - th is never the English 'th'. sh covers both ಶ and ಷ. v is a soft sound between English v and w. Double letters (nn, ll, tt, mm, chch) are held longer. jn stands for ಜ್ಞ, usually said 'gny'. f is used for ಫ in English loanwords.

The anusvara is written n or m according to how it sounds. English loanwords are romanised the way Kannada speakers say and spell them (bas, fon, daaktar, taim), not in their English spelling.

examples.english: it is good (ch, double n, long aa)
thank you (dh = d + breath; the last l is retroflex)
doctor (loanword, as Kannada speakers say it)

units.title: Greetings & basics
units.description: Say hello and goodbye, ask how someone is, thank people and give simple answers.

guide.title: One greeting for every time of day
guide.text:
ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ (namaskaara) works for hello and goodbye, morning or night, to anyone. ನಮಸ್ತೆ (namaste) is also understood. Kannada does have words for 'good morning' and 'good night' (shubhodaya, shubha raatri), but they are formal and sound like a radio announcer; in real life people say namaskaara, or just the English 'good morning'.

When leaving, Kannada speakers do not say 'I am going' - that sounds as if you will never return. They say ಹೋಗಿ ಬರ್ತೀನಿ (hogi barteeni), 'I will go and come back'. The person staying replies ಹೋಗಿ ಬನ್ನಿ (hogi banni), 'go and come'.

guide.title: How are you? - and how the words fuse
guide.text:
ಹೇಗೆ (hege) means 'how' and ಇದ್ದೀರ (iddeera) means 'you are'. Said together they fuse into one word: hege + iddeera = hegiddeera. In the same way the answer is ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿ (chennaagi, 'well') + ಇದ್ದೀನಿ (iddeeni, 'I am') = chennaagiddeeni. This fusing of a short word with 'is/am/are' happens all the time, so learn to hear the two parts.

ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿದ್ದೀರಾ? (chennaagiddeeraa?) with a long aa at the end is a yes/no question: 'Are you well?' The final -aa is the question marker. With a question word such as hege you do not need it.

ನೀವು (neevu) is the polite 'you' and is the one to use with adults you do not know well. To a child or a close friend you would say ನೀನು ಹೇಗಿದ್ದೀಯ? (neenu hegiddeeya?).

A very common friendly greeting around mealtimes is ಊಟ ಆಯ್ತಾ? - 'Have you eaten?' It is not an invitation; just answer ಆಯ್ತು (aaytu, 'done').

examples.english: How are you? (to a friend or child)

guide.title: Thank you, sorry and short answers
guide.text:
ಧನ್ಯವಾದಗಳು (dhanyavaadagalu) is 'thank you'. It is correct and appreciated, but among themselves people mostly say the English 'thanks', or show thanks with a smile and a polite verb form. ಕ್ಷಮಿಸಿ (kshamisi) is both 'sorry' and 'excuse me'.

ಹೌದು (haudu) is 'yes', ಇಲ್ಲ (illa) is 'no', and ಸರಿ (sari) is 'okay, right'. The unit 'Yes, no and polite words' looks at these more closely, because Kannada has three different words where English has 'no'.

phrases.note: Works at any time of day, for both hello and goodbye.
The first e is long. neevu is the polite 'you'. Often written with a long final vowel, ಹೇಗಿದ್ದೀರಾ; the formal written form is ಹೇಗಿದ್ದೀರಿ (hegiddeeri).
Spoken form; in writing it is chennaagiddene (ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿದ್ದೇನೆ).
The long -aa at the end makes it a yes/no question. Answer: ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿದ್ದೀನಿ (chennaagiddeeni).
In casual speech most people simply say 'thanks'.
Literally 'forgive (me)'.
Also means 'is not there'.
Also means 'correct'.
The o is long. The ending -ona means 'let us'.
Formal; many people just say 'good night'.
Formal - heard on the radio and in schools. The o is long.
The normal way to take leave: 'I'll go and come back'. Written form: hogi baruttene (ಹೋಗಿ ಬರುತ್ತೇನೆ).
What a host says to a guest. Written form of the second word: kulitukolli (ಕುಳಿತುಕೊಳ್ಳಿ).

units.title: Introductions
units.description: Introduce yourself, say where you are from and what you do, and ask the other person the same.

guide.title: 'I am X' needs no verb
guide.text:
To say that one thing is another, Kannada simply puts the two side by side: ನಾನು ವಿದ್ಯಾರ್ಥಿ (naanu vidyaarthi) is literally 'I student'. There is no word for 'am', 'is' or 'are' in this kind of sentence, and no word for 'a' or 'the'.

ನನ್ನ (nanna) is 'my' and ನಿಮ್ಮ (nimma) is 'your' (polite). So: nanna hesaru ... 'my name (is) ...'.

ಹೆಸರೇನು (hesarenu) is hesaru 'name' + enu 'what', fused: the final u of hesaru drops before the vowel. You can also say the two words separately: nimma hesaru enu?

guide.title: Where are you from? The endings -inda, -alli and -ge
guide.text:
Kannada has no separate words for 'from', 'in' and 'to'. They are endings on the noun: -inda 'from', -alli 'in', -ge or -kke 'to'. A linking sound is added where needed: amerika + inda = amerikadinda; bengalooru + alli = bengaloorinalli; illi 'here' + ge = illige 'to here'.

ನೀವು ಎಲ್ಲಿಯವರು? (neevu elliyavaru?) is the natural way to ask where someone is from: elli 'where' + -avaru 'person of'. The answer uses the same ending: ನಾನು ಬೆಂಗಳೂರಿನವನು (naanu bengaloorinavanu, said by a man) or ಬೆಂಗಳೂರಿನವಳು (bengaloorinavalu, said by a woman) - 'I am a Bengaluru person'. The simpler answer with -inda bandiddeeni ('I have come from ...') works for everyone.

ಊರು (ooru) means one's home town or native place; ನಿಮ್ಮ ಊರು ಯಾವುದು? is a favourite opening question.

examples.english: I am from America. (I have come from America.)
I live in Bengaluru. (I am in Bengaluru.)

guide.title: Introducing someone: the respectful plural
guide.text:
ಇವರು (ivaru) literally means 'these people', but it is the normal respectful way to point to one person: 'this gentleman / this lady'. The noun then also takes the plural ending -aru: snehita 'friend' becomes snehitaru. So ಇವರು ನನ್ನ ಸ್ನೇಹಿತರು can mean 'this is my friend' or 'these are my friends'.

Use ivaru for any adult you are introducing. The familiar forms ivanu (this boy/man) and ivalu (this girl/woman) are for children and close friends; they are taught in the unit on pronouns.

units.title: Yes, no and polite words
units.description: Agree, refuse, react and be polite with the short words Kannada speakers use all day.

guide.title: Three words for 'no'
guide.text:
English 'no' covers three different Kannada words, and choosing the right one is the first real step into the language.

ಇಲ್ಲ (illa) means 'is not there / does not exist / did not happen'. It is also the plain 'no' in answer to a question.

ಅಲ್ಲ (alla) means 'is not that'. Use it to say that something is not what was said: 'not this one', 'he is not a doctor', 'that is not right'.

ಬೇಡ (beda, long e) means 'not wanted / don't'. It refuses an offer: 'No, thank you'. Its opposite is ಬೇಕು (beku), 'wanted / needed'.

So: Is there tea? - illa. Is this tea? - alla. Do you want tea? - beda.

examples.english: Yes, I want it / It is needed

guide.title: Politeness is built into the verb
guide.text:
Kannada has a word for 'please', ದಯವಿಟ್ಟು (dayavittu), but it is formal - you hear it in announcements. In ordinary speech politeness comes from three things.

First, the verb ending. A request ending in -i is already polite: ಬನ್ನಿ (banni, 'please come'), ಕೊಡಿ (kodi, 'please give'). The bare form (baa, kodu) is only for children and close friends.

Second, the softener ಸ್ವಲ್ಪ (svalpa, 'a little'): svalpa jaaga bidi is 'make a little room, please'.

Third, how you address people. ಸಾರ್ (saar, 'sir') and ಮೇಡಂ (medam, 'madam') are used constantly. To strangers of roughly your own age people also say ಅಣ್ಣ (anna, 'elder brother') and ಅಕ್ಕ (akka, 'elder sister'), and to older people ಅಂಕಲ್ (ankal) and ಆಂಟಿ (aanti).

guide.title: Small words that keep a conversation moving
guide.text:
ಆಯ್ತು (aaytu) literally 'it happened', is the all-purpose 'all right, done, agreed'. ಸರಿ (sari) is 'okay, correct'. ಸಾಕು (saaku) is 'enough'. ಗೊತ್ತು (gottu) is 'known' - it is how you say 'I know'; its negative is ಗೊತ್ತಿಲ್ಲ (gottilla), gottu + illa.

Adding a long -aa turns any of these into a question: ಹೌದಾ? (haudaa?) 'Is that so?', ಸಾಕಾ? (saakaa?) 'Is that enough?', ಬೇಕಾ? (bekaa?) 'Do you want it?', ಗೊತ್ತಾ? (gottaa?) 'Do you know?'

ಪರವಾಗಿಲ್ಲ (paravaagilla) means 'it doesn't matter' and is the usual reply to both 'sorry' and 'thank you'.

units.title: Numbers 1-10
units.description: Count from zero to ten, count things and count people.

guide.title: Counting things
guide.text:
The numbers one to ten are ondu, eradu, mooru, naalku, aidu, aaru, elu, entu, ombattu, hattu. Watch the vowel lengths: mooru and aaru are long, elu (seven) has a long e but entu (eight) a short one, and hattu, ombattu have a doubled t.

The number comes before the noun, as in English. For things, the noun usually stays in the singular after a number: ಎರಡು ಟೀ (eradu tee) 'two teas', ಮೂರು ಮನೆ (mooru mane) 'three houses'. The plural ending -galu is possible (mooru manegalu) but is not needed in speech.

ಒಂದು (ondu) also does the work of 'a/an' when you want to stress 'one': ondu tee kodi, 'a tea, please'.

ಎಷ್ಟು (eshtu) asks both 'how many?' and 'how much?'.

guide.title: Counting people: special forms
guide.text:
Kannada counts people differently from things. For one and two people there are special words:

one man: ಒಬ್ಬ (obba); one woman: ಒಬ್ಬಳು (obbalu); one person, respectfully or when gender does not matter: ಒಬ್ಬರು (obbaru).

two people: ಇಬ್ಬರು (ibbaru).

Saying ondu or eradu for people is a typical learner's mistake: 'two children' is ibbaru makkalu, not eradu makkalu.

From three upwards the everyday way is the ordinary number plus ಜನ (jana, 'people'): mooru jana, naalku jana, hattu jana. Written Kannada also has ಮೂವರು (moovaru, three people) and ನಾಲ್ವರು (naalvaru, four people), which you will meet in reading.

guide.title: Kannada digits and zero
guide.text:
Kannada has its own digits: ೦ ೧ ೨ ೩ ೪ ೫ ೬ ೭ ೮ ೯. You will see them on bus number boards, calendars, some shop signs and government papers, so it is worth learning to recognise them - especially ೧ (1), ೨ (2), ೩ (3) and ೫ (5) for bus numbers. International digits are used just as often.

Zero is ಸೊನ್ನೆ (sonne). Phone numbers are read digit by digit, usually in English, but you will hear sonne, ondu, eradu too.

units.title: Word order and 'to be'
units.description: Build simple sentences: say what something is, where it is, and put the verb where Kannada wants it.

guide.title: The verb comes last
guide.text:
English says 'I eat rice': subject, verb, object. Kannada says 'I rice eat': subject, object, verb. The verb is always the last word of the sentence, and everything else lines up before it.

Words like 'to', 'in' and 'from' are not separate words placed before the noun; they are endings attached after it: ಶಾಲೆ (shaale) 'school', ಶಾಲೆಗೆ (shaalege) 'to school'. So 'He goes to school' is 'he school-to goes'.

The order of the pieces before the verb is fairly free, and the subject can be left out when the verb ending makes it obvious: ಹೋಗ್ತೀನಿ (hogteeni) alone means 'I am going', because -eeni can only be 'I'.

Kannada has no words for 'a' and 'the'.

examples.english: He goes to school. (he school-to goes)
I am going. / I will go.

guide.title: 'X is Y': no verb at all
guide.text:
When you say what something or someone is - a name, a job, a kind of thing - Kannada uses no verb. Just put the two side by side: ಇದು ಪುಸ್ತಕ (idu pustaka), 'this (is a) book'.

To make it negative add ಅಲ್ಲ (alla) at the end: ಇದು ಪುಸ್ತಕ ಅಲ್ಲ (idu pustaka alla), 'this is not a book'. alla never changes, whoever the subject is.

ಇದು (idu) is 'this (thing)' and ಅದು (adu) is 'that (thing)'.

guide.title: 'X is somewhere' and 'there is X': the verb iru
guide.text:
When you say where something is, or that something exists, you do need a verb: ಇರು (iru), 'to be (somewhere), to exist, to stay'. Its present forms change with the subject:

naanu iddeeni (I am), neenu iddeeya (you are, familiar), avanu iddaane (he is), avalu iddaale (she is), adu ide (it is), naavu iddeevi (we are), neevu iddeera (you are, polite or plural), avaru iddaare (they are; he or she is, respectful), avu ive (they are, of things).

The negative of all of these is the single word ಇಲ್ಲ (illa): avaru illa, 'he/she is not here'; neeru illa, 'there is no water'.

So Kannada separates two meanings of English 'is': 'is a doctor' (no verb, negative alla) and 'is at home' (iru, negative illa).

Written forms differ only slightly: iddene, iddeeya, iddaane, iddaale, ide, iddeve, iddeeri, iddaare, ive.

guide.title: Position words follow the noun
guide.text:
'On the table' is 'table's on': the noun takes the possessive ending and the position word comes after it. ಮೇಜು (meju) 'table' becomes ಮೇಜಿನ (mejina) 'of the table', then ಮೇಲೆ (mele) 'on, above'.

Useful position words: mele (on, above), kelage (under, below), olage (inside), horage (outside), hattira (near), munde (in front), hinde (behind). Several of them can also stand alone as adverbs: horage iddaare, 'they are outside'.

Short words often fuse with ide: illi + ide = illide (it is here), elli + ide = ellide (where is it?).

examples.english: The book is on the table.

units.title: Pronouns and respect
units.description: Say I, you, he, she, it, we and they, and choose the right level of respect.

guide.title: I, we and the two words for 'you'
guide.text:
ನಾನು (naanu) is 'I' and ನಾವು (naavu) is 'we'.

For 'you' there are two words. ನೀನು (neenu) is familiar: use it only with children, close friends of your own age, younger brothers and sisters - and people use it to God. ನೀವು (neevu) is polite, and is also the plural 'you all'. Use neevu with every adult you meet until they invite you to do otherwise; using neenu to a stranger, an elder or someone serving you is rude.

The verb changes to match: neenu takes endings in -eeya or the bare command form, neevu takes -eera and the polite command ending -i.

examples.english: You come. (to a child or friend)
Please come. (polite, or to several people)

guide.title: He, she and they: gender plus respect
guide.text:
The third person shows three things at once: near or far, male or female, and respect.

Far (that person): ಅವನು (avanu) he, ಅವಳು (avalu) she, ಅವರು (avaru) they. Near (this person here): ಇವನು (ivanu), ಇವಳು (ivalu), ಇವರು (ivaru). The first sound tells you: a- is 'that', i- is 'this'.

avanu and avalu are familiar, like neenu: use them for children, friends and younger relatives. For any adult you respect - parents, teachers, colleagues, strangers - use avaru, the plural, even for one person. The verb is then plural too: avaru iddaare, 'he/she is (here)'. Only context tells you whether avaru means 'he', 'she' or 'they'.

Respect matters more than gender here: a mother is avaru, not avalu.

guide.title: It and they for things: adu, idu, avu, ivu
guide.text:
Everything that is not a human being - objects, animals, ideas - is neuter in Kannada. There is no grammatical gender to memorise for nouns: a table is 'it', a dog is 'it'.

ಅದು (adu) is 'that, it' and ಇದು (idu) is 'this'. Their plurals are ಅವು (avu) 'those, they' and ಇವು (ivu) 'these'. A baby or small child is also often called adu, affectionately.

Neuter subjects take their own verb forms: adu ide (it is), avu ive (they are).

guide.title: Every pronoun has its own verb ending
guide.text:
Kannada verbs agree with the subject in person, number and - in the third person singular - gender. Here is 'to be (somewhere)' with each pronoun; the same endings appear on every verb in the language, so this table is worth learning by heart.

naanu iddeeni, neenu iddeeya, avanu iddaane, avalu iddaale, adu ide; naavu iddeevi, neevu iddeera, avaru iddaare, avu ive.

Notice the pattern: -eeni (I), -eeya (you familiar), -aane (he), -aale (she), -eevi (we), -eera (you polite), -aare (they / respectful he or she). The neuter forms ide and ive are the odd ones out.

examples.english: They are at home. / He or she is at home. (respectful)

units.title: My, your, his: possession
units.description: Say whose something is, with pronouns and with nouns.

guide.title: Possessive pronouns
guide.text:
Each pronoun has a possessive form that goes before the noun and never changes, whatever the noun is:

naanu - ನನ್ನ (nanna) my; naavu - ನಮ್ಮ (namma) our; neenu - ನಿನ್ನ (ninna) your, familiar; neevu - ನಿಮ್ಮ (nimma) your, polite or plural; avanu - ಅವನ (avana) his; avalu - ಅವಳ (avala) her; avaru - ಅವರ (avara) their, or his/her respectfully; adu - ಅದರ (adara) its, of that; idu - ಇದರ (idara) of this; yaaru - ಯಾರ (yaara) whose.

Kannada speakers very often say namma ('our') where English says 'my' - for home, family, town and country: namma mane ('our house', even if you live alone), namma appa ('our father' = my father), namma ooru, namma bengalooru. Saying nanna mane is not wrong, but namma sounds warmer and more natural.

examples.english: their house / his or her house (respectful)

guide.title: Possessive of nouns: the ending -a
guide.text:
A noun is made possessive (the 'of' or apostrophe-s form, called the genitive) by adding -a. The possessor comes first, as with English 's: appana kaaru, 'father's car'. A linking sound is needed, and it depends on how the noun ends:

People whose name or title ends in -a add -na: appa - ಅಪ್ಪನ (appana) father's; snehita - ಸ್ನೇಹಿತನ (snehitana) friend's; raama - raamana.

Things ending in -a add -da: mara - ಮರದ (marada) of the tree; pustaka - pustakada.

Nouns ending in -i or -e add -ya: mane - ಮನೆಯ (maneya) of the house; hudugi - hudugiya, the girl's.

Nouns ending in -u drop the u and add -ina: ooru - ಊರಿನ (oorina) of the town; bengalooru - bengaloorina. Words for people ending in -u just replace u with a: avanu - avana, magalu (daughter) - magala.

In fast speech the ending is often dropped where the meaning is clear: mane baagilu, 'the house door'.

guide.title: Mine, yours, whose: adding -du
guide.text:
To use a possessive on its own, without a noun after it ('mine', 'yours', 'Ravi's'), add -du, which stands for 'thing': ನನ್ನದು (nannadu) mine, ನಮ್ಮದು (nammadu) ours, ನಿನ್ನದು (ninnadu) and ನಿಮ್ಮದು (nimmadu) yours, ಅವನದು (avanadu) his, ಅವಳದು (avaladu) hers, ಅವರದು (avaradu) theirs, ಯಾರದು (yaaradu) whose.

To ask a yes/no question add the long -aa: nimmadu + aa = ನಿಮ್ಮದಾ? (nimmadaa?) 'Is it yours?'. To deny, add alla: nannadu alla, 'it is not mine'.

units.title: Case endings: to, from, in, with
units.description: Attach the seven case endings to nouns and pronouns to say to, from, in, by, of and to mark the object.

guide.title: Seven cases instead of prepositions
guide.text:
Where English puts a small word before the noun ('to the house', 'in the house'), Kannada adds an ending after it. Grammar books count seven cases (vibhakti):

1. Nominative - the subject. No ending; the noun appears in its basic form (mane).
2. Accusative - the object of the verb: -annu (maneyannu).
3. Instrumental - 'by, with, by means of': -inda (maneyinda).
4. Dative - 'to, for': -ge, -ige or -kke (manege).
5. Ablative - 'from'. Traditional grammar gives -deseyinda, but in real Kannada 'from' is also just -inda (maneyinda).
6. Genitive - 'of, 's': -a (maneya).
7. Locative - 'in, at, on': -alli (maneyalli).

There is also a calling form (vocative), used when addressing someone: amma becomes ammaa!, anna becomes annaa!

So in practice you need five endings: -annu, -inda, -ge/-kke, -a, -alli.

guide.title: Joining the ending: four kinds of noun
guide.text:
The ending is the same for every noun, but the sound that links it depends on the last vowel of the noun.

Nouns in -e or -i (mane, angadi, hudugi): link with y. maneyannu, maneyinda, maneya, maneyalli. The dative is simply -ge: manege, angadige.

Things in -a (mara 'tree', pustaka 'book'): link with v in the accusative and d elsewhere, and the dative is -kke. maravannu, maradinda, marakke, marada, maradalli.

People in -a (huduga 'boy', appa, amma, anna): link with n, and the dative is -nige. huduganannu, huduganinda, huduganige, hudugana. So ammanige is 'to Mother'.

Nouns in -u (ooru 'town', haalu 'milk', bassu 'bus'): the u drops. Accusative oorannu, dative oorige. The other cases insert -in-: oorininda, oorina, oorinalli. In speech the locative is often shortened to ooralli.

English loanwords ending in a consonant are treated as if they ended in -u: byaag - byaaginalli, aafees - aafeesige, bas - bassinalli.

guide.title: Pronouns with case endings
guide.text:
Pronouns take the same endings on their possessive stem. The dative forms are slightly irregular and are among the most used words in the language, so learn them first.

naanu: nannannu (me), nanninda (by/from me), nanage (to me), nanna (my), nannalli (in me).
neenu: ninnannu, ninninda, ninage, ninna.
neevu: nimmannu, nimminda, nimage, nimma.
naavu: nammannu, namminda, namage, namma.
avanu: avanannu, avaninda, avanige, avana.
avalu: avalannu, avalinda, avalige, avala.
avaru: avarannu, avarinda, avarige, avara.
adu: adannu, adarinda, adakke, adara, adaralli. idu is the same: idannu, idarinda, idakke, idara, idaralli.

Places: illi (here) - illige (to here), illinda (from here); alli - allige, allinda; elli - ellige (where to?), ellinda (where from?).

examples.english: to them / to him or her (respectful)

guide.title: When to use each ending
guide.text:
-annu marks the object, but only when it is a person or a definite thing: avarannu nodide, 'I saw them'; idannu tagolli, 'take this one'. An indefinite thing takes no ending: pustaka kodi, 'give (me) a book'. In speech -annu is usually shortened to -anna or -na (avaranna, idanna).

-ge / -kke marks the destination (manege, 'home'), the receiver (nanage kodi, 'give to me'), the purpose (pravaasakke, 'for a trip') and - very important - the person who feels, wants, knows or has something: nanage beku, 'I want'; nanage gottu, 'I know'.

-inda is 'from' a place or time (aafeesininda), 'by means of' a tool (chamachadinda, 'with a spoon') and 'because of' (maleyinda, 'because of the rain').

-alli is 'in, at, on' for place (maneyalli) and also 'by' for transport (bassinalli, 'by bus').

guide.title: 'With', 'near', 'under': words after the genitive
guide.text:
Other relations are expressed by a separate word placed after the possessive (genitive) form of the noun:

ಜೊತೆ (jote) with, together with: nanna jote, 'with me'; snehitana jote, 'with a friend'.
ಹತ್ತಿರ (hattira) near, and also 'in the possession of': maneya hattira, 'near the house'.
ಮೇಲೆ (mele) on; ಕೆಳಗೆ (kelage) under; ಒಳಗೆ (olage) inside; ಮುಂದೆ (munde) in front of; ಹಿಂದೆ (hinde) behind; ಪಕ್ಕ (pakka) beside.

Note that 'with' meaning 'using' is -inda (chamachadinda), while 'with' meaning 'together with' is jote.

phrases.note: Dative -ge for the destination. Written: hoguttene (ಹೋಗುತ್ತೇನೆ).
-inda = from. Written: baruttene (ಬರುತ್ತೇನೆ).
maisooru + in + alli. Spoken shortcut: maisooralli (ಮೈಸೂರಲ್ಲಿ).
nanage = to me.
-annu marks a person as object. In speech: avaranna (ಅವರನ್ನ).
Transport takes -alli: literally 'in the bus'.
People ending in -a take -nige. The e of heli is long.
jote follows the possessive form.
-inda also means 'by means of'.

phrases.english: I have to go to the shop.
phrases.note: angadi + ge.

phrases.english: How far is it from Bengaluru to Mysuru?
phrases.note: 'From' and 'to' in one sentence.
Written: idannu tegedukolli (ತೆಗೆದುಕೊಳ್ಳಿ).

phrases.english: The key is in the bag.
phrases.note: A loanword ending in a consonant takes -inalli, like a noun in -u.

units.title: Asking questions
units.description: Ask yes/no questions with -aa and open questions with what, who, where, when, why, how and how much.

guide.title: Yes/no questions: add a long -aa
guide.text:
To turn any statement into a yes/no question, add a long -aa to its last word. Nothing else changes - no word order change, no 'do' or 'is'.

If the last word ends in u, the u drops: beku - ಬೇಕಾ? (bekaa?), gottu - ಗೊತ್ತಾ? (gottaa?), nimmadu - ನಿಮ್ಮದಾ? (nimmadaa?).

If it ends in e or i, a linking y appears: ide - ಇದೆಯಾ? (ideyaa?), bandide - bandideyaa? The one exception is the spoken neuter ending -utte, whose final e is simply replaced by -aa: barutte - ಬರುತ್ತಾ? (baruttaa?), hogutte - hoguttaa?

If it ends in a, the a simply lengthens: barteera - ಬರ್ತೀರಾ? (barteeraa?), illa - ಇಲ್ಲವಾ? (illavaa?) or in speech ಇಲ್ವಾ? (ilvaa?).

The answer is haudu (yes) or illa (no), or more naturally just the verb repeated: barteeraa? - barteeni.

guide.title: Question words
guide.text:
The question words mostly begin with e- or yaa-:

ಏನು (enu) what; ಯಾರು (yaaru) who; ಎಲ್ಲಿ (elli) where; ಯಾವಾಗ (yaavaaga) when; ಯಾಕೆ (yaake) why; ಹೇಗೆ (hege) how; ಎಷ್ಟು (eshtu) how much, how many; ಯಾವ (yaava) which (before a noun); ಯಾವುದು (yaavudu) which one.

The question word stays where the answer would be - usually just before the verb. It does not jump to the front as in English: neevu elli iddeera? 'you where are?'.

A sentence with a question word does not take the -aa ending.

yaake is the spoken word for 'why'; in writing you will see ಏಕೆ (eke).

examples.english: Who is he / she? Who are they?

guide.title: Question words take case endings too
guide.text:
Because question words stand in for nouns, they take the same endings as nouns:

elli (where) - ಎಲ್ಲಿಗೆ (ellige) where to; ಎಲ್ಲಿಂದ (ellinda) where from.
yaaru (who) - ಯಾರಿಗೆ (yaarige) to whom; ಯಾರನ್ನು (yaarannu) whom; ಯಾರ (yaara) whose; ಯಾರ ಜೊತೆ (yaara jote) with whom.
enu (what) - ಏನನ್ನು (enannu) what (as object, rarely needed); ಯಾವುದಕ್ಕೆ (yaavudakke) for what.
eshtu (how much) - ಎಷ್ಟಕ್ಕೆ (eshtakke) for how much; ಎಷ್ಟು ಗಂಟೆಗೆ (eshtu gantege) at what time.

A question word plus -oo gives 'any / every' words: yaaroo (anyone, no one with a negative), enoo (anything), elloo (anywhere), yaavaagaloo (always).

examples.english: Who should I give this to?

guide.title: Isn't it? and either/or
guide.text:
ಅಲ್ವಾ? (alvaa?) at the end of a sentence is the tag question 'isn't it? / right?'. It is alla + -aa; the written form is ಅಲ್ಲವಾ (allavaa) or ಅಲ್ಲವೇ (allave). It works for every person and tense.

For 'A or B?' put -aa on both choices: tee bekaa, kaafi bekaa? 'Do you want tea, or do you want coffee?'

In writing, yes/no questions often use the ending -ಏ (-e) or -ಆ (-aa) interchangeably: ಇದೆಯೇ? (ideye?) = ideyaa?

examples.english: Do you want tea or coffee?

phrases.note: nimmadu + -aa; the u drops.
Statement: barteera; question: barteeraa.
Answer: gottu (yes, I do) or gottilla (no, I don't).
Also 'Who are they?'
ellige = elli + ge, 'to where'.
Written: bandiri (ಬಂದಿರಿ).
Written form: eke (ಏಕೆ).
maadodu ('the doing') is the spoken form of maaduvudu (ಮಾಡುವುದು).
Written: hoguttade (ಹೋಗುತ್ತದೆ).
What a shopkeeper or waiter asks.
alvaa works as a tag after any statement.

phrases.english: Do you want tea or coffee?
phrases.note: Either/or: put -aa on both choices.
ellinda = elli + inda.

units.title: Saying no: negation
units.description: Say that something is not so, is not there, did not happen, is not wanted or must not be done.

guide.title: illa and alla
guide.text:
ಇಲ್ಲ (illa) is the negative of iru, 'to be (somewhere), to exist'. It says that something or someone is not present or does not exist, and it is the same for every person: naanu illa, avaru illa, neeru illa.

ಅಲ್ಲ (alla) is the negative of the verbless 'X is Y' sentence. It says that something is not what was claimed: naanu daaktar alla, 'I am not a doctor'; idu sari alla, 'this is not right'.

A quick test: if the positive sentence would use ide / iddaare, the negative is illa. If the positive sentence has no verb, the negative is alla.

With question-word + -oo, a negative gives 'nobody, nothing, nowhere': yaaroo illa (nobody is here), enoo illa (there is nothing), elloo illa (it is nowhere).

examples.english: He / She is not at home.

guide.title: Negating a verb: -alla and -alilla
guide.text:
Negative verbs are wonderfully simple in spoken Kannada, because they do not change with the person.

Don't / doesn't / won't: verb stem + -alla. maadu - ಮಾಡಲ್ಲ (maadalla), hogu - ಹೋಗಲ್ಲ (hogalla), baa - ಬರಲ್ಲ (baralla), tinnu - ತಿನ್ನಲ್ಲ (tinnalla), kudi - ಕುಡಿಯಲ್ಲ (kudiyalla), nodu - ನೋಡಲ್ಲ (nodalla), kelu - ಕೇಳಲ್ಲ (kelalla), kodu - ಕೊಡಲ್ಲ (kodalla), iru - ಇರಲ್ಲ (iralla), aagu - ಆಗಲ್ಲ (aagalla). naanu baralla, avanu baralla, avaru baralla: I, he, they won't come. The written form is the verbal noun + illa: maaduvudilla, baruvudilla.

Didn't: verb stem + -alilla (the infinitive in -alu plus illa). ಮಾಡಲಿಲ್ಲ (maadalilla), ಹೋಗಲಿಲ್ಲ (hogalilla), ಬರಲಿಲ್ಲ (baralilla), ತಿನ್ನಲಿಲ್ಲ (tinnalilla), ಕೊಡಲಿಲ್ಲ (kodalilla), ಆಗಲಿಲ್ಲ (aagalilla). Again one form for all persons. In fast speech the a drops: maadlilla, barlilla.

Isn't / aren't ...-ing: stem + -tilla. ಬರ್ತಿಲ್ಲ (bartilla) is not coming; ಮಾಡ್ತಿಲ್ಲ (maadtilla) is not doing; ಆಗ್ತಿಲ್ಲ (aagtilla) is not happening.

guide.title: Don't! and must not
guide.text:
A negative command is the verb stem + -a + ಬೇಡ (beda): ಹೋಗಬೇಡ (hogabeda), 'don't go', to a friend or child. For the polite form add -i: ಹೋಗಬೇಡಿ (hogabedi). Likewise maadabedi (don't do), barabedi (don't come), mareyabedi (don't forget).

A rule or prohibition - 'one must not, it is not allowed' - uses stem + -a + ಬಾರದು (baaradu): illi nillisabaaradu, 'one must not stop here'. This is what you see on signs.

In fast speech the linking a is dropped: hogbedi, maadbedi, maadbaardu.

examples.english: Don't go. (to a friend or child)

guide.title: Negatives of want, know, like and can
guide.text:
Several everyday words have their own negative partner:

ಬೇಕು (beku) want/need - ಬೇಡ (beda) don't want.
ಗೊತ್ತು (gottu) know - ಗೊತ್ತಿಲ್ಲ (gottilla) don't know.
ಇಷ್ಟ (ishta) like - ಇಷ್ಟ ಇಲ್ಲ (ishta illa) don't like.
ಬರುತ್ತೆ (barutte) 'comes' = know how to - ಬರಲ್ಲ (baralla) can't, don't know how.
ಆಗುತ್ತೆ (aagutte) 'happens' = is possible - ಆಗಲ್ಲ (aagalla) can't be done, not possible.
ಸಾಕು (saaku) enough - ಸಾಲಲ್ಲ (saalalla) not enough.

All of these take the person in the dative: nanage beda, nanage gottilla, nanage baralla.

phrases.note: illa is the same for every person.
alla, not illa: you are denying what you are.
Written: tinnuvudilla (ತಿನ್ನುವುದಿಲ್ಲ).
Written: baruvudilla (ಬರುವುದಿಲ್ಲ).
Fast speech: barlilla (ಬರ್ಲಿಲ್ಲ).
enu + -oo = enoo, 'anything'.
To a friend or child: hogabeda (ಹೋಗಬೇಡ).
gaadi is any vehicle. -baaradu states a rule.
A language 'comes to you' in Kannada.
yaaru + -oo = yaaroo.
Written: baruttilla (ಬರುತ್ತಿಲ್ಲ).

units.title: This, that, here, there
units.description: Point to things, places, amounts and ways of doing something, near and far.

guide.title: The i- / a- / e- system
guide.text:
Kannada pointing words come in neat sets of three. A word beginning with i- points to something near ('this'), the same word beginning with a- points to something far ('that'), and with e- or yaa- it asks a question ('which?').

Thing: ಇದು (idu) this - ಅದು (adu) that - ಯಾವುದು (yaavudu) which one / ಏನು (enu) what.
Place: ಇಲ್ಲಿ (illi) here - ಅಲ್ಲಿ (alli) there - ಎಲ್ಲಿ (elli) where.
Time: ಈಗ (eega) now - ಆಗ (aaga) then - ಯಾವಾಗ (yaavaaga) when.
Manner: ಹೀಗೆ (heege) like this - ಹಾಗೆ (haage) like that - ಹೇಗೆ (hege) how.
Amount: ಇಷ್ಟು (ishtu) this much - ಅಷ್ಟು (ashtu) that much - ಎಷ್ಟು (eshtu) how much.
Person: ivanu / avanu, ivalu / avalu, ivaru / avaru - yaaru.

Learn one column and you know all three.

guide.title: ee and aa before a noun; idu and adu on their own
guide.text:
English uses 'this' both before a noun ('this house') and alone ('this is a house'). Kannada uses two different words.

Before a noun use the long vowels ಈ (ee) 'this' and ಆ (aa) 'that'. They never change: ee mane (this house), ee manegalu (these houses), aa hudugi (that girl).

Standing alone as the subject or object use ಇದು (idu) and ಅದು (adu), with plurals ಇವು (ivu) 'these' and ಅವು (avu) 'those': idu mane, 'this is a house'.

So ee mane chennaagide is 'this house is nice', but idu chennaagide is 'this is nice'.

examples.english: I want this one, not that one.

guide.title: Endings on pointing words, and the emphatic -e
guide.text:
The place words take case endings directly: illige (to here), illinda (from here), allige (to there), allinda (from there).

idu and adu take endings on the stems ida- and ada-: idannu (this, as object), idakke (to/for this), idara (of this), idaralli (in this), idakkinta (than this).

A long -e added to almost any word means 'only, itself, the very': ಇಲ್ಲೇ (ille) right here; ಅಲ್ಲೇ (alle) right there; ಈಗಲೇ (eegale) right now; ಅದೇ (ade) that very one, the same; ಇದೇ (ide) this very one; ಇವತ್ತೇ (ivatte) today itself. This little ending is extremely common in speech.

ಆಮೇಲೆ (aamele) literally 'on top of that' means 'afterwards, later'.

phrases.note: ee before a noun; idu when standing alone.

phrases.english: I want this one, not that one.

phrases.note: The o of nodi is long.
Shoes are left at the door of homes and temples.
heege (like this) has a long ee; hege (how) has a long e.
illi + emphatic -e; the final e is long.
adu + emphatic -e.

units.title: Describing things
units.description: Describe people and things, say 'very' and 'a little', and compare two things.

guide.title: Adjectives go before the noun and never change
guide.text:
A Kannada adjective stands before its noun, as in English, and it does not change for gender, number or case. ದೊಡ್ಡ (dodda) 'big' stays dodda in dodda mane (big house), dodda manegalu (big houses), dodda maneyalli (in the big house).

Common adjectives: ದೊಡ್ಡ (dodda) big; ಚಿಕ್ಕ (chikka) small; ಒಳ್ಳೆಯ (olleya) good; ಕೆಟ್ಟ (ketta) bad; ಹೊಸ (hosa) new; ಹಳೆಯ (haleya) old (of things); ಬಿಸಿ (bisi) hot; ಉದ್ದ (udda) long, tall.

In speech olleya and haleya are shortened to olle and hale: olle huduga, 'a good boy'.

Colours: ಕೆಂಪು (kempu) red; ಬಿಳಿ (bili) white; ಕಪ್ಪು (kappu) black; ಹಸಿರು (hasiru) green; ನೀಲಿ (neeli) blue; ಹಳದಿ (haladi) yellow. ಬಣ್ಣ (banna) is 'colour'.

guide.title: 'The house is big': add -du or a person ending
guide.text:
When the adjective is the last word of the sentence ('is big'), it cannot stand bare. It is turned into a noun meaning 'a big one'.

For things add -ದು (-du): doddadu (a big one), chikkadu (a small one), hosadu (a new one), haleyadu (an old one), olleyadu (a good one). ee mane doddadu = 'this house (is) a big one'.

For people add the pronoun endings: -ವನು (-vanu) for a man, -ವಳು (-valu) for a woman, -ವರು (-varu) for respect or plural: olleyavanu (a good man), olleyavalu (a good woman), olleyavaru (a good person / good people).

Many descriptions are not adjectives at all but a noun or adverb plus ide: bisi ide (is hot), doora ide (is far), chennaagide (is good, from chennaagi 'well' + ide), tannagide (is cold, from tannage + ide). Words like sulabha (easy), kashta (difficult), ettara (tall, height), dubaari (expensive) are used as they are, with no ending and no verb: idu sulabha.

examples.english: He / She is a very good person.

guide.title: Comparing: -ginta
guide.text:
Kannada adjectives have no '-er' or 'more' form. To compare, add the ending -ಗಿಂತ (-ginta), 'than', to the thing you are comparing with, and leave the adjective alone: 'this that-than big' = 'this is bigger than that'.

-ginta attaches like the dative ending: adu - ಅದಕ್ಕಿಂತ (adakkinta) than that; idu - idakkinta; naanu - ನನಗಿಂತ (nanaginta) than me; neevu - nimaginta; avanu - avaniginta; maisooru - ಮೈಸೂರಿಗಿಂತ (maisooriginta) than Mysuru; mane - maneginta.

For 'the most' compare with 'all': ಎಲ್ಲಕ್ಕಿಂತ (ellakkinta) 'than everything' for things, ಎಲ್ಲರಿಗಿಂತ (ellariginta) 'than everyone' for people.

To say 'more' and 'less' of something, use ಜಾಸ್ತಿ (jaasti) and ಕಡಿಮೆ (kadime).

examples.english: This is the smallest of all.

guide.title: Very, a little, too much
guide.text:
ತುಂಬಾ (tumbaa) 'very, a lot' goes before the adjective: tumbaa dodda, tumbaa chennaagide.

ಸ್ವಲ್ಪ (svalpa) is 'a little, somewhat': svalpa doora, 'a bit far'.

ಜಾಸ್ತಿ (jaasti) is 'more, too much': khaara jaasti, 'too spicy'. ಕಡಿಮೆ (kadime) is 'less, too little': sakkare kadime, 'less sugar'.

ಇನ್ನೂ (innoo) is 'still, even more': innoo dodda, 'even bigger'.

phrases.note: At the end of a sentence dodda needs -du.

phrases.english: He is a very good person.
phrases.note: For a boy: olleyavanu; for a girl: olleyavalu.
tannage (coldly) + ide.
haleya is 'old' for things only. An old person is vayassaadavaru (ವಯಸ್ಸಾದವರು).

phrases.english: This is the smallest of all.

units.title: Present tense: what you do
units.description: Conjugate any verb in the present for every person, and talk about habits and plans.

guide.title: One tense for 'I do' and 'I will do' - singular
guide.text:
The Kannada present tense (more exactly the 'non-past') covers habits ('I work'), general truths, and the near future ('I'll do it'). The verb is built from the stem + t + a personal ending.

The dictionary form of a verb is its stem, which is also the familiar command: ಮಾಡು (maadu) 'do, make'. In speech the final u drops before the t: maad- + teeni = maadteeni.

The singular endings: -teeni (I), -teeya (you, familiar), -taane (he), -taale (she). The neuter 'it' form keeps the u and ends in -utte: maadutte.

Written Kannada uses fuller forms with -utt-: maaduttene, maadutteeya, maaduttaane, maaduttaale, maaduttade. If you can say the spoken forms you will recognise these at once.

examples.english: I do / I will do. (written: maaduttene)

guide.title: Plural and respectful forms
guide.text:
The plural endings: -teevi (we), -teera (you, polite or plural), -taare (they; and he or she when you speak respectfully). Things in the plural take -tave.

Remember that avaru + -taare is what you use for any single adult you respect: amma aduge maadtaare, 'Mother cooks'.

Written forms: maadutteve (we), maadutteeri (you), maaduttaare (they), maaduttave (they, things).

For the polite 'you', a statement ends in short -a (maadteera) and a yes/no question in long -aa (maadteeraa?). You will also hear and see -teeri, which is closer to the written form.

examples.english: They do. / He or she does. (respectful; written: maaduttaare)

guide.title: The ten most useful verbs
guide.text:
Most verbs end in -u and behave exactly like maadu. Here are ten essential verbs with their 'I' form and their 'it' form:

ಮಾಡು maadu (do): maadteeni, maadutte.
ಹೋಗು hogu (go): hogteeni, hogutte.
ನೋಡು nodu (see, look): nodteeni, nodutte.
ಕೇಳು kelu (ask, listen): kelteeni, kelutte.
ಕೊಡು kodu (give): kodteeni, kodutte.
ಆಗು aagu (become, happen): aagteeni, aagutte.
ಇರು iru (be, stay): irteeni, irutte.
ಬಾ baa (come): irregular stem bar-: barteeni, barutte.
ತಿನ್ನು tinnu (eat): the stem shortens to tin-: tinteeni (spelled ತಿಂತೀನಿ), but tinnutte.
ಕುಡಿ kudi (drink): verbs ending in -i or -e lengthen that vowel: kudeeteeni (ಕುಡೀತೀನಿ), but kudiyutte. The same happens with kali (learn): kaleeteeni; bare (write): bareeteeni; kare (call): kareeteeni; nade (walk): nadeeteeni.

Every one of these then takes the full set of endings: hogteeni, hogteeya, hogtaane, hogtaale, hogutte, hogteevi, hogteera, hogtaare.

Note on iru: 'I am (now)' is iddeeni, the special form you already know. irteeni means 'I will be / I usually am': naale maneyalli irteeni, 'I'll be at home tomorrow'.

guide.title: Noun + maadu: making new verbs
guide.text:
A huge number of everyday actions are a noun followed by maadu, 'do': kelasa maadu (do work = to work), aduge maadu (do cooking = to cook), oota maadu (do meal = to eat a meal), sahaaya maadu (do help = to help), snaana maadu (to bathe), nidde maadu (to sleep), fon maadu (to phone). English words slot in the same way: draiv maadu, 'to drive'.

So once you can conjugate maadu, you can say hundreds of things.

Words such as ದಿನಾ (dinaa) 'every day', ಯಾವಾಗಲೂ (yaavaagaloo) 'always' and ಬೆಳಿಗ್ಗೆ (beligge) 'in the morning' mark the habitual meaning.

phrases.note: maataadu = to speak, talk. Written: maataaduttene (ಮಾತಾಡುತ್ತೇನೆ).

phrases.english: What do you do? (to a friend)
phrases.note: Familiar form. Polite: neevu enu maadteera?
Written: hoguttaane (ಹೋಗುತ್ತಾನೆ).
Written: hoguttaale (ಹೋಗುತ್ತಾಳೆ).

phrases.english: We drink tea in the evening.
phrases.note: Written: kudiyutteve (ಕುಡಿಯುತ್ತೇವೆ).
Written: maadutteeri (ಮಾಡುತ್ತೀರಿ).

phrases.english: He gets up early in the morning.
phrases.note: elu (long e) = to get up - the same spelling as 'seven'. Written: eluttaare (ಏಳುತ್ತಾರೆ).
Neuter form in -utte. Written: nilluttade (ನಿಲ್ಲುತ್ತದೆ).

phrases.english: I go for a walk every day.
phrases.note: dinaa = every day (from dina, day).
Plural verb for respect.
Written: kudiyuttaare (ಕುಡಿಯುತ್ತಾರೆ).
Animals take the neuter form. Written: tinnuttade (ತಿನ್ನುತ್ತದೆ).

phrases.english: I go to bed at ten at night.
phrases.note: malagu = to lie down, go to sleep.
Long -aa makes it a question.
The person helped is in the dative: nanage.

units.title: Happening now
units.description: Say what you and others are doing right now, and what was going on at some time in the past.

guide.title: am / is / are doing: stem + -t- + the forms of iru
guide.text:
For an action in progress, Kannada joins the verb stem + t(aa) to the present forms of iru, 'to be': maadtaa iddeeni, literally 'doing I-am'. In normal speech this is pronounced and written as one word: ಮಾಡ್ತಿದ್ದೀನಿ (maadtiddeeni).

Since you already know iddeeni, iddeeya, iddaane, iddaale, ide, you already know the endings.

Written forms: maaduttiddene (I), maaduttiddeeya (you), maaduttiddaane (he), maaduttiddaale (she), maaduttide (it).

Compare: naanu kelasa maadteeni, 'I work / I will work'; naanu kelasa maadtiddeeni, 'I am working (right now)'.

guide.title: Plural and respectful forms
guide.text:
The plural follows iru in the same way: -tiddeevi (we), -tiddeera (you, polite), -tiddaare (they / respectful), -tive (they, of things).

Written forms: maaduttiddeve, maaduttiddeeri, maaduttiddaare, maaduttive.

The stems are the same ones you learned for the present: hogtiddeeni (I am going), bartiddeeni (I am coming), nodtiddeeni (I am watching), odtiddeeni (I am reading). The -i and -e verbs keep their long vowel: kudeetiddeeni (I am drinking), kaleetiddeeni (I am learning). tinnu gives tintiddeeni (ತಿಂತಿದ್ದೀನಿ), 'I am eating'.

examples.english: They are doing. / He or she is doing. (respectful)

guide.title: Not doing, are you doing?, was doing
guide.text:
Negative: stem + -tilla, the same for every person: ಮಾಡ್ತಿಲ್ಲ (maadtilla) 'am / is / are not doing'; bartilla, 'not coming'. Written: maaduttilla.

Question: add -aa as always. bartide - bartideyaa? 'is it coming?'; maadtiddeera - maadtiddeeraa? 'are you doing?'.

Was doing: replace the present of iru with its past (idde, idde, idda, idlu, ittu, idvi, idri, idru): ಮಾಡ್ತಿದ್ದೆ (maadtidde) I was doing; maadtidda, he was doing; maadtittu, it was doing; maadtidru, they were doing.

One trap: states that English expresses with '-ing' or an adjective are often a completed action in Kannada. 'He is sleeping / asleep' is malagiddaane, literally 'he has lain down'; 'she is sitting' is kootiddaale, 'she has sat'.

examples.english: He is asleep. (he has lain down)

phrases.note: Written: maaduttiddene (ಮಾಡುತ್ತಿದ್ದೇನೆ).
Written: maaduttiddeeri (ಮಾಡುತ್ತಿದ್ದೀರಿ).
A state: Kannada says 'has lain down', not 'is sleeping'.

phrases.english: She is talking on the phone.

phrases.note: Rain 'comes' in Kannada. Written: baruttide (ಬರುತ್ತಿದೆ).
kaayu = to wait. Written: kaayuttiddeve (ಕಾಯುತ್ತಿದ್ದೇವೆ).
aata = game, aadu = to play.
Also said to mean 'I'm on my way'.

phrases.english: Where are you going? (to a friend)
phrases.note: Familiar form.
-tilla is the same for all persons.
odu (long o) = to read, to study.
bartide + y + aa.
Past continuous: -tidde. Written: maaduttidde (ಮಾಡುತ್ತಿದ್ದೆ).
Plural verb for respect.

units.title: Past tense: what happened
units.description: Talk about what you did, using regular verbs and the common irregular ones.

guide.title: Regular past: stem + id + ending (singular)
guide.text:
The past tense is the past stem + a personal ending. For the many regular verbs in -u, the past stem is the verb without its u, plus -id-: maadu - maadid-.

The singular endings are: -e (I), -e (you, familiar), -a (he), -lu (she), and -tu for 'it'.

naanu maadide and neenu maadide are identical; the pronoun tells them apart. For 'he', the short form maadida is what you say; the written form adds -nu: maadidanu. 'She' is maadidlu in speech and maadidalu (ಮಾಡಿದಳು) in writing. 'It' is maaditu (ಮಾಡಿತು).

Other regular verbs: nodu - nodide (I saw); kelu - kelide (I asked, heard); helu - helide (I said); maataadu - maataadide (I spoke); odu - odide (I read); torisu - toriside (I showed).

guide.title: Plural and respectful forms
guide.text:
The plural endings in speech are: -vi (we), -ri (you, polite or plural), -ru (they / respectful he or she). So: maadidvi, maadidri, maadidru.

The written forms have an extra vowel: maadidevu (ಮಾಡಿದೆವು) we did; maadidiri (ಮಾಡಿದಿರಿ) you did; maadidaru (ಮಾಡಿದರು) they did. The neuter plural is maadidavu in both.

Since respected people take the plural, 'Father said' is appa helidru.

examples.english: They did. / He or she did. (respectful; written: maadidaru)

guide.title: Irregular past stems to learn by heart
guide.text:
The commonest verbs have irregular past stems. The endings are the regular ones; only the stem and the 'it' form must be memorised. Each line gives: I, he, she, it, we, you (polite), they.

ಹೋಗು hogu (go) - stem hod-: hode, hoda, hodlu, hoytu, hodvi, hodri, hodru.
ಬಾ baa (come) - stem band-: bande, banda, bandlu, bantu, bandvi, bandri, bandru.
ತಿನ್ನು tinnu (eat) - stem tind-: tinde, tinda, tindlu, tintu, tindvi, tindri, tindru.
ಕುಡಿ kudi (drink) - stem kudid-: kudide, kudida, kudidlu, kudiyitu, kudidvi, kudidri, kudidru.
ಕೊಡು kodu (give) - stem kott-: kotte, kotta, kotlu, kottitu, kotvi, kotri, kotru.
ಇರು iru (be) - stem idd-: idde, idda, idlu, ittu, idvi, idri, idru.
ಆಗು aagu (become, happen) - stem aad-: aade, aada, aadlu, aaytu, aadvi, aadri, aadru.

The 'you, familiar' form is always the same as the 'I' form: neenu hode, neenu bande.

Written forms keep the dropped vowel: hodalu, hoyitu, hodevu, hodiri, hodaru; bandalu, banditu, bandevu, bandiri, bandaru; kottalu, kottevu, kottiri, kottaru; iddalu, iddevu, iddiri, iddaru; aayitu.

More irregular pasts you will meet soon: nillu (stand, stop) - ninte; kootko (sit) - kootkonde; tago (take) - tagonde; elu (get up) - edde; beelu (fall) - bidde; kali (learn) - kalite; bare (write) - barede; mare (forget) - marete; sigu (be found, be got) - sikkitu.

guide.title: The neuter past and 'it happened'
guide.text:
The neuter ('it') forms are the least regular and the most used, because weather, time, work, events and things are all neuter.

ಆಯ್ತು (aaytu) 'it happened, it is done' - written ಆಯಿತು (aayitu). kelasa aaytu, 'the work is done'; oota aaytu, 'the meal is over (I have eaten)'.
ಹೋಯ್ತು (hoytu) 'it went, it is gone' - written ಹೋಯಿತು (hoyitu).
ಬಂತು (bantu) 'it came' - written ಬಂದಿತು (banditu). male bantu, 'it rained'.
ಇತ್ತು (ittu) 'it was, there was'. chali ittu, 'it was cold'.
ಸಿಕ್ಕಿತು (sikkitu) 'it was found, (I) got it'.

The negative past is the same for all persons and all verbs: stem + -alilla (baralilla, 'didn't come'; sigalilla, 'didn't get'). 'There was not' is ಇರಲಿಲ್ಲ (iralilla).

phrases.note: Written: maadidenu (ಮಾಡಿದೆನು).
maadide + y + aa. In fast speech: maadidyaa? (ಮಾಡಿದ್ಯಾ?). Polite: neevu oota maadidraa? (ಮಾಡಿದ್ರಾ?)
Written: hodanu (ಹೋದನು).
Written: kottalu (ಕೊಟ್ಟಳು).
Written: bandaru (ಬಂದರು).
Written: nodidevu (ನೋಡಿದೆವು).
Written: tindiri (ತಿಂದಿರಿ).
Written: banditu (ಬಂದಿತು).
Written: aayitu (ಆಯಿತು).

phrases.english: I was there for two years.
phrases.note: No word for 'for' is needed with a length of time.
Written: helidaru (ಹೇಳಿದರು).
kelu means both 'ask' and 'listen, hear'.
ittu is the neuter past of iru.
sigu = to be found, to be available; the person is in the dative.

units.title: Future, plans and suggestions
units.description: Say what you will do, suggest doing something together, offer to do something and say what may happen.

guide.title: The everyday future is the present tense
guide.text:
Spoken Kannada has no separate future tense. The present forms you already know do the job, usually helped by a time word: naanu naale barteeni, 'I come tomorrow' = 'I will come tomorrow'.

Time words for the future: ನಾಳೆ (naale) tomorrow; ನಾಡಿದ್ದು (naadiddu) the day after tomorrow; ಆಮೇಲೆ (aamele) later, afterwards; ಮುಂದಿನ ವಾರ (mundina vaara) next week; ಇನ್ನು ಐದು ನಿಮಿಷದಲ್ಲಿ (innu aidu nimishadalli) in five minutes.

The full set once more, with baa (come): barteeni, barteeya, bartaane, bartaale, barutte, barteevi, barteera, bartaare.

The negative future is the same -alla form as the negative present: baralla, 'won't come'; aagalla, 'won't happen / can't be done'.

For 'will be' use iru: irteeni (I will be), irutte (it will be). For 'will become / will happen' use aagu: aagutte.

examples.english: They will come in the evening.

guide.title: Let's ... and Shall I ...?
guide.text:
'Let's do it' is the verb stem + -ಓಣ (-ona, long o): ಹೋಗೋಣ (hogona) let's go; ಮಾಡೋಣ (maadona) let's do; ನೋಡೋಣ (nodona) let's see; ಸಿಗೋಣ (sigona) let's meet; ಬರೋಣ (barona) let's come. As a question: hogonaa? 'shall we go?'.

'Shall I ...? / May I ...?' is the verb stem + -ಅಲಾ (-alaa): ಬರಲಾ? (baralaa?) shall I come?; ಹೋಗಲಾ? (hogalaa?) shall I go?; ಕೊಡಲಾ? (kodalaa?) shall I give?; ಮಾಡಲಾ? (maadalaa?) shall I do it? This is the polite way to offer or to ask permission.

With a question word the same form ends in -ali: ಏನು ಮಾಡಲಿ? (enu maadali?) 'What shall I do?'; ಏನು ಕೊಡಲಿ? (enu kodali?) 'What shall I give you?'

examples.english: Shall I come? / May I come in?

guide.title: May, might: -abahudu
guide.text:
To say that something may happen, or that someone may do something, add -ಅಬಹುದು (-abahudu) to the verb stem. It does not change with the person.

ಬರಬಹುದು (barabahudu) may come; ಆಗಬಹುದು (aagabahudu) may happen; ಇರಬಹುದು (irabahudu) may be; ಹೋಗಬಹುದು (hogabahudu) may go.

The same form gives permission: neevu hogabahudu, 'you may go'. As a question it asks permission: hogabahudaa? 'may I go?'.

ಬಹುಶಃ (bahushah) 'perhaps' often goes with it.

guide.title: The written future tense (for reading)
guide.text:
Written and formal Kannada does have a future tense, formed with -uv- between the stem and the ending. You will meet it in books, songs, speeches and news, but people do not use it in conversation.

maadu: naanu maaduvenu, neenu maaduve, avanu maaduvanu, avalu maaduvalu, adu maaduvudu, naavu maaduvevu, neevu maaduviri, avaru maaduvaru, avu maaduvuvu.

Other verbs follow the same pattern: hoguvenu (I shall go), baruvenu (I shall come), koduvenu (I shall give), iruvenu (I shall be), aaguvudu (it will happen).

The word maaduvudu also serves as the verbal noun 'doing', which is why the written negative is maaduvudilla, 'doing is-not'.

phrases.note: Present form + naale = future.

phrases.english: We'll go to Mysuru next week.
phrases.note: Written: hogutteve (ಹೋಗುತ್ತೇವೆ).

phrases.english: They will come in the evening.
phrases.note: Written: baruttaare (ಬರುತ್ತಾರೆ).
fon maadu = to phone.
Both o are long. Question: hogonaa? (ಹೋಗೋಣಾ?) 'shall we go?'
Also said at a door for 'May I come in?' and when leaving for 'Shall I go now?'
Written: aaguttade (ಆಗುತ್ತದೆ).
maneyalli + emphatic -e. Written: iruttene (ಇರುತ್ತೇನೆ).
vaapas baa = come back.
Written: heluttaane (ಹೇಳುತ್ತಾನೆ).
Also a polite way of saying 'I'll think about it'.

phrases.english: I'll be there in five minutes.

phrases.note: The -alla negative covers present and future.

units.title: Requests and commands
units.description: Ask people to do things politely, tell friends and children what to do, and say 'don't'.

guide.title: Familiar and polite commands
guide.text:
The bare verb stem is the command to someone you call neenu - a child, a close friend: maadu (do!), hogu (go!), nodu (look!), kodu (give!).

For everyone else, and for more than one person, replace the final -u with -i. This form is already polite and needs no 'please': ಮಾಡಿ (maadi), ಹೋಗಿ (hogi), ನೋಡಿ (nodi), ಕೇಳಿ (keli), ಕೊಡಿ (kodi), ಹೇಳಿ (heli), ಇರಿ (iri).

Two very common verbs are irregular:
baa (come) - ಬನ್ನಿ (banni).
taa (bring) - ತನ್ನಿ (tanni).
(tinnu, 'eat', is regular - ತಿನ್ನಿ (tinni) - and only looks like them.)

Verbs ending in -i or -e add -yiri: kudi (drink) - ಕುಡಿಯಿರಿ (kudiyiri); kare (call) - ಕರೆಯಿರಿ (kareyiri); bare (write) - ಬರೆಯಿರಿ (bareyiri); tere (open) - ತೆರೆಯಿರಿ (tereyiri). In speech these are shortened: kudeeri, kareeri.

Verbs ending in -ko (the short spoken form of -kollu) take -kolli: kootko (sit) - ಕೂತ್ಕೊಳ್ಳಿ (kootkolli); tago (take) - ತಗೊಳ್ಳಿ (tagolli).

examples.english: Come here. (to a friend or child)

guide.title: Softening a request
guide.text:
The -i form is polite, but a bare command can still sound abrupt. Kannada speakers soften requests in several ways:

ಸ್ವಲ್ಪ (svalpa) 'a little' before the verb: svalpa iri, 'wait a bit, please'; svalpa nodi, 'have a look, would you'.

An address word: saar, medam, anna, akka.

A question instead of a command: svalpa sahaaya maadteeraa? 'will you help a little?'; ee kelasa maadoke aaguttaa? 'would it be possible to do this?'

ದಯವಿಟ್ಟು (dayavittu) 'please' is for formal situations and written notices.

Adverbs of manner go before the verb: ಬೇಗ (bega) quickly; ನಿಧಾನವಾಗಿ (nidhaanavaagi) slowly; ಜೋರಾಗಿ (joraagi) loudly, fast; ಮೆಲ್ಲಗೆ (mellage) softly, gently.

guide.title: Don't, and 'let him'
guide.text:
Negative command: verb stem + -a + ಬೇಡ (beda) for neenu, + ಬೇಡಿ (bedi) for neevu. maadabeda / maadabedi (don't do), hogabedi (don't go), mareyabedi (don't forget), helabedi (don't tell). Verbs in -i and -e insert y: mare - mareyabedi; kudi - kudiyabedi.

'Let him / her / it / them ...' is the stem + -ಅಲಿ (-ali): ಬರಲಿ (barali) let him come; ಇರಲಿ (irali) let it be - a very common word meaning 'never mind, leave it'; ಆಗಲಿ (aagali) let it be so - a polite 'very well'.

For 'let's' use -ona (hogona) and for 'shall I' use -alaa (baralaa?), as in the unit on the future.

phrases.english: Come here. (to a friend or child)
phrases.note: Familiar. Polite: illi banni.
iru = be, stay, wait.
In speech: idanna nodi (ಇದನ್ನ ನೋಡಿ).
maatu = word, speech.
In everyday speech people also say tegeeri (ತೆಗೀರಿ) for 'open'.
Spoken short form: kudeeri (ಕುಡೀರಿ).
The e of bega is long.
What you say to a driver who is going too fast.
idu = to put, keep. (Do not confuse with idu, 'this', which has a dental d.)
mare (forget) + y + a + bedi.
Familiar. Polite: maadabedi.
torisu = to show; the o is long.

units.title: Want, need, can, must
units.description: Say what you want, what you have to do, what you can and cannot do, and what is allowed.

guide.title: Wanting a thing: dative + beku
guide.text:
'I want water' is ನನಗೆ ನೀರು ಬೇಕು (nanage neeru beku), literally 'to-me water is-wanted'. The person who wants is in the dative (nanage, nimage, avanige, avalige, avarige, namage), the thing wanted is the subject, and ಬೇಕು (beku) never changes.

beku covers both 'want' and 'need'.

Negative: ಬೇಡ (beda) - nanage beda, 'I don't want (it)'. A softer 'I don't need it' is ಬೇಕಾಗಿಲ್ಲ (bekaagilla).
Question: ಬೇಕಾ? (bekaa?) - nimage enu beku? 'what do you want?'; neeru bekaa? 'do you want water?'
Past: ಬೇಕಿತ್ತು (bekittu) 'wanted, was needed' - also a polite way to ask in a shop: nanage ondu pen bekittu, 'I was wanting a pen'.

This 'dative subject' pattern - the person in the dative, the feeling or thing as subject - is one of the keys to Kannada. You will meet it again with knowing, liking, having, being hungry and being ill.

examples.english: I wanted a pen. / I'd like a pen.

guide.title: Having to do something: verb + -abeku
guide.text:
Attach beku to a verb stem with a linking -a- and you get 'must, have to, need to, should': ಹೋಗಬೇಕು (hogabeku) must go; ಮಾಡಬೇಕು (maadabeku) must do; ಬರಬೇಕು (barabeku) must come; ತಿನ್ನಬೇಕು (tinnabeku) must eat; ನೋಡಬೇಕು (nodabeku) must see; ಕೊಡಬೇಕು (kodabeku) must give; ಇರಬೇಕು (irabeku) must be. Verbs in -i and -e insert y: kudiyabeku (must drink), iliyabeku (must get down).

The form is the same for every person. The person is usually in the plain form (naanu hogabeku); with the dative (nanage hogabeku) the sense leans towards 'I want to go'.

Stronger: insert the emphatic -e: ಬರಲೇಬೇಕು (baralebeku) 'really must come'.

Negatives - three different meanings:
needn't: ಬರಬೇಕಾಗಿಲ್ಲ (barabekaagilla), 'there is no need to come'.
don't (command): ಬರಬೇಡಿ (barabedi).
must not, shouldn't: ಬರಬಾರದು (barabaaradu).

Past: ಹೋಗಬೇಕಿತ್ತು (hogabekittu) 'had to go / should have gone'.

examples.english: You must not take photos here.

guide.title: Can: knowing how (barutte) and being able (aagutte)
guide.text:
Kannada separates two kinds of 'can'.

A skill you have learned 'comes to you': dative + skill + ಬರುತ್ತೆ (barutte). nanage kannada barutte, 'I can speak Kannada (Kannada comes to me)'. With a verb, use the -oke form: nanage eejoke barutte, 'I know how to swim'. Negative: ಬರಲ್ಲ (baralla). You will also hear barutte pronounced baratte.

Being able to do something on a given occasion 'happens for you': dative + verb in -oke + ಆಗುತ್ತೆ (aagutte). nanage baroke aagutte, 'I can come (it is possible for me)'. Negative: ಆಗಲ್ಲ (aagalla) - nanage baroke aagalla, 'I can't come'. Past: aaytu / aagalilla, 'managed to / couldn't'.

The -oke form ('to do, for doing') is made by adding -ಓಕೆ (-oke) to the stem: maadoke, hogoke, baroke, tinnoke, nodoke, odoke, kodoke; verbs in -i and -e insert y: kudiyoke, bareyoke. In written Kannada it is the infinitive in -alu: maadalu, baralu - so 'I can't come' is written nanage baralu aaguvudilla.

guide.title: May (permission) and liking
guide.text:
Permission and possibility use -ಅಬಹುದು (-abahudu), 'may, can': neevu illi kootkollabahudu, 'you may sit here'. To ask permission add -aa: ಬರಬಹುದಾ? (barabahudaa?) 'may I come?'. The refusal is -baaradu.

Liking is another dative pattern: dative + thing + ಇಷ್ಟ (ishta), 'liking'. nanage dose ishta, 'I like dosa'. Negative: ishta illa. To like doing something, use the -odu form of the verb (the spoken verbal noun, 'the doing'): nanage ododu ishta, 'I like reading'; nanage aduge maadodu ishta, 'I like cooking'.

phrases.note: beku = want or need. The e is long.
enaadaroo = anything at all. In speech: enaadroo (ಏನಾದ್ರೂ).
Fast speech: hogbeku (ಹೋಗ್ಬೇಕು).
The inserted long -e- adds insistence - a warm way to invite someone.
'Needn't' - different from barabedi, 'don't come'.
Written: nanage kannada odalu baruttade (ಓದಲು ಬರುತ್ತದೆ).
eeju = to swim.
Written: baralu aaguvudilla (ಬರಲು ಆಗುವುದಿಲ್ಲ).
A polite way to ask a favour.

phrases.english: You must not take photos here.
phrases.note: foto tege = to take a photo.
The o of dose is long.
With the dative nanage the sense is 'I feel the need to'.

units.title: Have and have not
units.description: Say what you have and do not have: relatives, things, time, money and ailments.

guide.title: There is no verb 'to have'
guide.text:
Kannada says 'to me there is ...' or 'near me there is ...'. The verb is iru (ide, iddaane, iddaale, iddaare, ive), and it agrees with the thing possessed, not with the owner.

Pattern 1 - dative + iru. Used for relatives, friends, time, work, questions, feelings, illnesses, and anything that is not a physical object you carry: nanage obba tamma iddaane, 'to me one younger-brother is' = 'I have a younger brother'; nanage samaya ide, 'I have time'; nanage talenovu ide, 'I have a headache'.

Because the verb agrees with what is possessed: obba tamma iddaane (he is), obbalu akka iddaale (she is), ibbaru makkalu iddaare (they are), ondu prashne ide (it is).

When counting relatives, remember the human number words: obba / obbalu, ibbaru, mooru jana.

guide.title: Things you own or have on you: hattira
guide.text:
Pattern 2 - possessive + ಹತ್ತಿರ (hattira, 'near') + iru. Used for objects and money that you own or have with you: nanna hattira hana ide, 'near me money is' = 'I have money'; avana hattira baik ide, 'he has a motorbike'.

In fast speech hattira is shortened to hatra (ಹತ್ರ): nan hatra hana ide.

The written language also uses ಬಳಿ (bali) in the same way: nanna bali hana ide.

For what a place has, use the locative: namma maneyalli eradu naayi ive, 'in our house there are two dogs' = 'we have two dogs'.

examples.english: We have two dogs at home.

guide.title: Not having, and having in the past
guide.text:
The negative is ಇಲ್ಲ (illa) in place of the form of iru, for every person and number: nanage samaya illa, 'I have no time'; nanna hattira chillare illa, 'I have no change'.

Question: ideyaa? / iddaaraa? - nimma hattira pen ideyaa? 'do you have a pen?'; nimage makkalu iddaaraa? 'do you have children?'. In a question with eshtu the verb is often left out: nimage eshtu makkalu? 'how many children do you have?'

Past: ಇತ್ತು (ittu) for things, ಇದ್ದ (idda) / ಇದ್ಲು (idlu) / ಇದ್ರು (idru) for people; negative ಇರಲಿಲ್ಲ (iralilla). nanna hattira kaaru ittu, 'I had a car'; nanage samaya iralilla, 'I had no time'.

phrases.note: In speech also duddu (ದುಡ್ಡು) for money, and hatra (ಹತ್ರ) for hattira.
Useful with auto drivers and at small shops.
obba = one (male person); the verb is masculine.
obbalu = one (female person); the verb is feminine. Many speakers would use the respectful iddaare for an elder sister.
Written: moovaru makkalu (ಮೂವರು ಮಕ್ಕಳು).
People also say taim illa (ಟೈಮ್ ಇಲ್ಲ).
tale (head) + novu (pain); the o is long.

phrases.english: We have two dogs at home.
phrases.note: ive is the neuter plural of ide.

phrases.english: How many children do you have?
phrases.note: The verb iddaare can be left out.
Can also mean 'she has no work to do (just now)'.

units.title: Linking actions and helper verbs
units.description: Chain actions together ('go and come', 'eat and see'), say 'have done', and use the helper verbs that give Kannada its flavour.

guide.title: The 'having done' form
guide.text:
Kannada does not join verbs with 'and'. Instead, every verb except the last is put in a short form meaning 'having done' (the verbal participle), and only the final verb carries tense and person: oota maadi banni, 'having-done meal, come' = 'eat and then come'.

How to form it:
Regular verbs in -u change -u to -i: maadu - ಮಾಡಿ (maadi); hogu - ಹೋಗಿ (hogi); nodu - ನೋಡಿ (nodi); kelu - ಕೇಳಿ (keli); helu - ಹೇಳಿ (heli); aagu - ಆಗಿ (aagi). (This looks the same as the polite command; the position in the sentence tells you which it is.)

Verbs with an irregular past use the past stem + u: baa - ಬಂದು (bandu); tinnu - ತಿಂದು (tindu); kudi - ಕುಡಿದು (kudidu); kodu - ಕೊಟ್ಟು (kottu); iru - ಇದ್ದು (iddu); tago - ತಗೊಂಡು (tagondu); kootko - ಕೂತ್ಕೊಂಡು (kootkondu); nillu - ನಿಂತು (nintu); elu - ಎದ್ದು (eddu); bare - ಬರೆದು (baredu); mare - ಮರೆತು (maretu).

Several can be chained: angadige hogi, haalu tagondu, bega baa - 'go to the shop, get milk and come back quickly'.

examples.english: I'll go to the shop and come back.
Bring some milk. (take milk and come)

guide.title: 'Have done': participle + iru
guide.text:
Add the present of iru to the participle and you get the perfect, 'have done': maadi + iddeeni = ಮಾಡಿದ್ದೀನಿ (maadiddeeni), 'I have done'.

maadiddeeni, maadiddeeya, maadiddaane, maadiddaale, maadide, maadiddeevi, maadiddeera, maadiddaare.

With irregular verbs: bandiddeeni (I have come), hogiddaare (they have gone), tindiddeeni (I have eaten), kottiddeeni (I have given), nodiddeeni (I have seen), bandide (it has come).

Careful with the look-alikes: maadide can be 'I did' (past) or 'it has done' (perfect neuter). Context decides.

Negative: participle + illa: ಬಂದಿಲ್ಲ (bandilla) hasn't come; ಮಾಡಿಲ್ಲ (maadilla) haven't done; ನೋಡಿಲ್ಲ (nodilla) haven't seen. Same for all persons.

With the past of iru you get 'had done': bandidde, 'I had come'.

Written forms: maadiddene, bandiddaare, bandide.

examples.english: They have gone to their home town.

guide.title: Helper verbs after the participle
guide.text:
A participle followed by certain common verbs gives shades of meaning that English expresses with adverbs or not at all. The helper loses its own meaning.

ಬಿಡು (bidu, 'leave') - completely, once and for all, get it over with: maadibidi, 'get it done'; hogibidi, 'just go'; maretubitte, 'I clean forgot'; tindubitta, 'he ate it all up'.

ಕೊಳ್ಳು (kollu, spoken ko, 'take') - do it for oneself: tagolli, 'take (for yourself)'; kootkolli, 'sit yourself down'; nodkolli, 'look after it / see for yourself'; its 'I' form is -kolteeni: nodkolteeni, 'I'll take care of it'.

ಕೊಡು (kodu, 'give') - do it for someone else: helikodi, 'tell-give' = teach, explain; maadikodi, 'do it for me'; torisikodi, 'show me how'.

ನೋಡು (nodu, 'see') - try: tindu nodi, 'eat and see' = taste it; maadi nodi, 'try doing it'; keli nodi, 'try asking'.

ಹೋಗು (hogu, 'go') - something happens by itself, often unwanted: kaleduhogide, 'it has got lost'; mugiduhoytu, 'it got finished / used up'; haalaagihoytu, 'it got spoiled'.

guide.title: 'Without doing': the negative participle
guide.text:
The opposite of 'having done' is 'without doing': verb stem + -ಅದೆ (-ade). maadu - ಮಾಡದೆ (maadade) without doing; hogu - hogade; helu - ಹೇಳದೆ (helade) without saying; baa - barade; tinnu - tinnade; nodu - nodade.

avanu enoo helade hoda, 'he went without saying anything'; oota maadade hogabedi, 'don't go without eating'.

With iru it makes a negative command or habit: barade irabedi, 'don't fail to come'.

phrases.english: I'll go to the shop and come back.
Bring some milk. (to a friend or child)
phrases.note: 'Bring' is 'take and come'; 'take away' is tagondu hogu. Written: tegedukondu (ತೆಗೆದುಕೊಂಡು).
Written: maadiddene (ಮಾಡಿದ್ದೇನೆ).

phrases.english: They have gone to their home town.

phrases.note: Spoken short form: maretbitte (ಮರೆತ್ಬಿಟ್ಟೆ).
helikodu = to teach, explain to someone.
Written: nodikolluttene (ನೋಡಿಕೊಳ್ಳುತ್ತೇನೆ).
mugi = to end. Written: mugiduhoyitu (ಮುಗಿದುಹೋಯಿತು).
Written: kulitukondu (ಕುಳಿತುಕೊಂಡು).
bandu + ide.

units.title: Food & drink
units.description: Order in a restaurant, ask for things at the table and talk about food.

guide.title: Ordering: number + item + kodi
guide.text:
To order, say how many, what, and ಕೊಡಿ (kodi), 'please give': ondu tee kodi, 'one tea, please'; eradu masaale dose kodi, 'two masala dosas, please'. You can also say nanage ... beku, 'I want ...'.

ಹಾಕಿ (haaki) 'put' is used for anything added or served onto the plate: khaara kadime haaki, 'put less chilli'; innoo svalpa saambaar haaki, 'put a little more sambar'.

To stop someone serving you more, say ಸಾಕು (saaku), 'enough'. To refuse, ಬೇಡ (beda).

Useful words: ನೀರು (neeru) water; ಬಿಸಿ ನೀರು (bisi neeru) hot water; ಹಾಲು (haalu) milk; ಸಕ್ಕರೆ (sakkare) sugar; ಉಪ್ಪು (uppu) salt; ಅನ್ನ (anna) cooked rice; ಮೊಸರು (mosaru) curd, yoghurt; ತರಕಾರಿ (tarakaari) vegetables; ಹಣ್ಣು (hannu) fruit.

guide.title: Hunger, thirst and taste
guide.text:
Hunger and thirst 'happen to you', so the person is in the dative: nanage hasivaagide, 'to me hunger has happened' = 'I am hungry' (hasivu 'hunger' + aagide). nanage baayaarike aagide, 'I am thirsty'.

Taste words: ಖಾರ (khaara) spicy, hot with chilli; ಸಿಹಿ (sihi) sweet; ಹುಳಿ (huli) sour; ಕಹಿ (kahi) bitter; ಉಪ್ಪು (uppu) salt, salty; ಬಿಸಿ (bisi) hot in temperature; ರುಚಿ (ruchi) taste.

To praise food: ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿದೆ (chennaagide) 'it is good' or ರುಚಿಯಾಗಿದೆ (ruchiyaagide) 'it is tasty'. chennaagirutte, with irutte instead of ide, means 'is (generally) good' - the form to use when asking for a recommendation.

ನಾನು ಸಸ್ಯಾಹಾರಿ (naanu sasyaahaari) is 'I am vegetarian'. In everyday speech people say 'vej' and 'naan-vej'.

guide.title: Meals and the question 'Have you eaten?'
guide.text:
ಊಟ (oota) is a full meal - lunch or dinner, normally with rice. ತಿಂಡಿ (tindi) is breakfast or a snack: idli, dosa, vada and so on. 'To eat a meal' is oota maadu; 'to have breakfast' is tindi tinnu or tindi maadu.

ಊಟ ಆಯ್ತಾ? (oota aaytaa?), 'Is your meal done?', is a standard friendly greeting around midday or in the evening; in the morning it is ತಿಂಡಿ ಆಯ್ತಾ? (tindi aaytaa?). The usual answer is ಆಯ್ತು (aaytu), 'done' - and then you ask back: nimdu? ('yours?').

A guest is always pressed to eat more. ಸಾಕು, ಇನ್ನು ಬೇಡ (saaku, innu beda), 'enough, no more', said with a hand over the plate, is the polite way out.

phrases.note: hasivu (hunger) + aagide.
The verb ending -i is already polite, so no separate 'please' is needed.
In Bengaluru tea is 'tee'; in north Karnataka you will hear 'chahaa' (ಚಹಾ).
The o of dose is long.
irutte (rather than ide) for what is generally true. Written: chennaagiruttade (ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿರುತ್ತದೆ).
A compliment every cook likes to hear.
Non-vegetarian: maamsaahaari (ಮಾಂಸಾಹಾರಿ).
Tea and coffee normally come already sweetened, so say this when ordering.
innoo = still, more.
Often fused: idenu? (ಇದೇನು?)

phrases.english: That's enough, I don't want any more.
phrases.note: saaku = enough; beda (long e) = don't want.
Literally 'Is your meal done?' - a very common friendly greeting.

units.title: Directions & getting around
units.description: Ask where things are, understand directions and guide an auto or cab driver.

guide.title: Where is ...? How far?
guide.text:
