'Where is X?' is X + ಎಲ್ಲಿದೆ? (ellide?), which is elli 'where' + ide 'is'. For a person use elliddaare?

'How far?' is ಎಷ್ಟು ದೂರ? (eshtu doora?). 'From here' is ಇಲ್ಲಿಂದ (illinda). 'Near' is ಹತ್ತಿರ (hattira); 'far' is ದೂರ (doora).

Answers you will hear: ಇಲ್ಲೇ (ille) right here; ಹತ್ತಿರದಲ್ಲೇ (hattiradalle) very near; ಸ್ವಲ್ಪ ದೂರ (svalpa doora) a bit far; ಎರಡು ಕಿಲೋಮೀಟರ್ (eradu kilomeetar) two kilometres; ಐದು ನಿಮಿಷ (aidu nimisha) five minutes.

Place names take -ge or -kke for 'to': maisoorige, jayanagarakke, steshange. English place words ending in a consonant simply add -ge in speech.

examples.english: How far is it from here?

guide.title: Left, right, straight
guide.text:
ಎಡ (eda) is 'left' and ಬಲ (bala) is 'right'. With the 'to' ending they become ಎಡಕ್ಕೆ (edakke) 'to the left' and ಬಲಕ್ಕೆ (balakke) 'to the right'. 'On the left side' is ಎಡಗಡೆ (edagade), 'on the right side' ಬಲಗಡೆ (balagade). In Bengaluru drivers very often use the English words left and right, with Kannada verbs.

ನೇರವಾಗಿ (neravaagi) or ನೇರ (nera) is 'straight'. ಮುಂದೆ (munde) is 'ahead, in front'; ಹಿಂದೆ (hinde) 'behind, back'; ಪಕ್ಕ (pakka) 'beside, next to'; ಎದುರು (eduru) 'opposite'.

Verbs: ಹೋಗಿ (hogi) go; ತಿರುಗಿ (tirugi) turn; ನಿಲ್ಲಿಸಿ (nillisi) stop (the vehicle); ಬನ್ನಿ (banni) come.

guide.title: Autos, cabs and buses
guide.text:
To hail an auto-rickshaw, name the place with -ge / -kke and ask ಬರ್ತೀರಾ? (barteeraa?), 'will you come?': mejestikge barteeraa? The driver answers banni ('come') or names a price.

ಮೀಟರ್ ಹಾಕಿ (meetar haaki) is 'put the meter on'. ಎಷ್ಟು ಆಗುತ್ತೆ? (eshtu aagutte?) is 'how much will it come to?'.

'I want to go to X' is naanu X-ge hogabeku. On a bus, ask the conductor: ee bas X-ge hoguttaa? 'does this bus go to X?'. To get off, say illi ilisi, 'let me down here'.

ಇಳಿ (ili) is 'get down, get off' and ಹತ್ತು (hattu) is 'climb, get on' - yes, the same word as 'ten'.

examples.english: I want to go to the airport.

phrases.note: The formal Kannada word is railu nildaana (ರೈಲು ನಿಲ್ದಾಣ).
A large bus station is bas styaand (ಬಸ್ ಸ್ಟ್ಯಾಂಡ್).

phrases.english: How far is it from here?

phrases.note: Both the e in ne and the o in ho are long.
Said to a driver. nillisu = to stop something; nillu = to stop, stand.

phrases.english: I want to go to the airport.
phrases.note: In everyday speech people usually just say 'airport': erportge (ಏರ್‌ಪೋರ್ಟ್‌ಗೆ).
How to ask an auto driver. Majestic is Bengaluru's central bus and rail hub.
In cities people often say 'toilet ellide?'
daari = way, road.
Adding -aa to the end of a sentence makes it a yes/no question.
nadedukondu hogu = to go on foot. Spoken: nadkondu (ನಡ್ಕೊಂಡು).

units.title: Shopping, numbers 11-100 and money
units.description: Count to a hundred and beyond, ask prices, bargain and pay.

guide.title: Eleven to nineteen
guide.text:
The teens are built on hattu (ten), which shrinks to han- or hadi- in front of the unit:

11 hannondu, 12 hanneradu, 13 hadimooru, 14 hadinaalku, 15 hadinaidu, 16 hadinaaru, 17 ಹದಿನೇಳು (hadinelu, long e), 18 ಹದಿನೆಂಟು (hadinentu), 19 ಹತ್ತೊಂಬತ್ತು (hattombattu).

Notice that 19 keeps the full hattu: hattu + ombattu.

guide.title: The tens
guide.text:
The tens end in -vattu or -pattu (a worn-down hattu):

20 ippattu, 30 moovattu, 40 nalavattu, 50 aivattu, 60 aravattu, 70 eppattu, 80 ಎಂಬತ್ತು (embattu), 90 ತೊಂಬತ್ತು (tombattu), 100 ನೂರು (nooru).

Take care with the similar-sounding pairs: eppattu (70) and embattu (80); ombattu (9) and tombattu (90).

1,000 is ಸಾವಿರ (saavira); 100,000 is ಲಕ್ಷ (laksha), the 'lakh' used all over India; ten million is ಕೋಟಿ (koti), a 'crore'.

guide.title: Putting numbers together
guide.text:
Tens and units join into one word, ten first, and the final u of the ten drops before a vowel (sandhi again): ippattu + ondu = ippattondu (21); ippattu + aidu = ippattaidu (25); moovattu + aaru = moovattaaru (36); nalavattu + eradu = nalavatteradu (42). Before a consonant the u becomes a: ಇಪ್ಪತ್ತಮೂರು (ippattamooru) 23, ಇಪ್ಪತ್ತನಾಲ್ಕು (ippattanaalku) 24; in fast speech that a is swallowed: ippatmooru, ippatnaalku.

Hundreds: 100 nooru, 200 ಇನ್ನೂರು (innooru), 300 ಮುನ್ನೂರು (munnooru), 400 ನಾನೂರು (naanooru), 500 ಐನೂರು (ainooru), then aarunooru, elunooru, entunooru, ombainooru. A hundred plus something is noora ...: ನೂರ ಐವತ್ತು (noora aivattu) 150, usually run together as nooraivattu.

Thousands: eradu saavira (2,000), hattu saavira (10,000).

guide.title: Prices and bargaining
guide.text:
The rupee is ರೂಪಾಯಿ (roopaayi). The noun stays singular after a number: nooru roopaayi, 'a hundred rupees'.

To ask a price: idara bele eshtu? ('what is the price of this?') or simply ಇದು ಎಷ್ಟು? (idu eshtu?), 'how much is this?'. For produce sold by weight: keji eshtu? 'how much a kilo?'.

'For a hundred rupees' uses the dative: nooru roopaayige kodi, 'give it for a hundred'.

Bargaining words: ದುಬಾರಿ (dubaari) expensive; ಜಾಸ್ತಿ (jaasti) too much; ಕಡಿಮೆ ಮಾಡಿ (kadime maadi) reduce it; ಕೊನೆ ಬೆಲೆ (kone bele) last price. In markets and with street vendors bargaining is expected; in shops with fixed prices it is not.

ಒಟ್ಟು (ottu) is 'total'; ಚಿಲ್ಲರೆ (chillare) is 'small change'.

examples.english: Please reduce the price a little.
Give it for a hundred rupees.

guide.title: Halves, quarters and weights
guide.text:
ಅರ್ಧ (ardha) is 'half': ardha keji, 'half a kilo'. ಕಾಲು (kaalu) is 'a quarter' (and also 'leg'); ಮುಕ್ಕಾಲು (mukkaalu) is 'three quarters'.

'And a half' is -ವರೆ (-vare) joined to the number, whose final u lengthens to oo: ಒಂದೂವರೆ (ondoovare) one and a half; ಎರಡೂವರೆ (eradoovare) two and a half; mooroovare, three and a half.

Weights and measures use the English words: ಕೆಜಿ (keji) kilo; ಗ್ರಾಂ (graam) gram; ಲೀಟರ್ (leetar) litre. A dozen is ಡಜನ್ (dajan) - bananas are sold by the dozen.

phrases.note: In shops people often just say 'idu eshtu?' (ಇದು ಎಷ್ಟು?).

phrases.english: Please reduce the price a little.
phrases.note: The standard bargaining phrase.
'nanage ... beku' = 'I want / need ...'. The e in beku is long.

phrases.english: Do you have a bigger size?
phrases.note: idakkinta = than this. For 'smaller': chikka (ಚಿಕ್ಕ).
bere (long e) = other, different.
Literally 'Do you take cards?' (spoken form). Written: tegedukollutteeraa? (ತೆಗೆದುಕೊಳ್ಳುತ್ತೀರಾ?)
In Bengaluru shops a carry bag is often called 'kavar' (ಕವರ್).
summane = just, for no particular reason.
ippattu + aidu.

phrases.english: Give it for a hundred rupees.
phrases.note: The dative -ge gives 'for (a price)'.

phrases.english: Half a kilo of tomatoes, please.
phrases.note: No word for 'of'.
eshtu + aaytu.

units.title: Family
units.description: Name your relatives, introduce them and answer the questions everyone will ask about your family.

guide.title: Older or younger? Kannada always says
guide.text:
Kannada has no plain word for 'brother' or 'sister'. You must say whether the person is older or younger than you:

ಅಣ್ಣ (anna) elder brother; ತಮ್ಮ (tamma) younger brother; ಅಕ್ಕ (akka) elder sister; ತಂಗಿ (tangi) younger sister.

Parents and grandparents: ಅಪ್ಪ (appa) father; ಅಮ್ಮ (amma) mother; ತಾತ (taata) or ಅಜ್ಜ (ajja) grandfather; ಅಜ್ಜಿ (ajji) grandmother. The formal words ತಂದೆ (tande) father and ತಾಯಿ (taayi) mother are used in writing and on forms.

Marriage and children: ಗಂಡ (ganda) husband; ಹೆಂಡತಿ (hendati) wife; ಮಗ (maga) son; ಮಗಳು (magalu) daughter; ಮಗು (magu) child, baby; ಮಕ್ಕಳು (makkalu) children.

Uncles and aunts depend on the side of the family and on age. Father's elder brother is ದೊಡ್ಡಪ್ಪ (doddappa, 'big father'), his younger brother ಚಿಕ್ಕಪ್ಪ (chikkappa, 'small father'); mother's elder sister is ದೊಡ್ಡಮ್ಮ (doddamma), her younger sister ಚಿಕ್ಕಮ್ಮ (chikkamma). Mother's brother is ಮಾವ (maava) and father's sister is ಅತ್ತೆ (atte) - these two words also mean father-in-law and mother-in-law.

guide.title: Respect inside the family
guide.text:
Elders are spoken about with avaru / ivaru and a plural verb, even your own parents: ivaru nanna amma, 'this is my mother'; appa bartaare, 'Father is coming'; nanna taata halliyalli iddaare, 'my grandfather is in the village'.

Younger relatives take the singular: nanna tamma kaalejige hogtaane; nanna tangi odtiddaale.

For an elder brother or sister both are heard; the plural is the safer, more polite choice.

Husband and wife: introducing a spouse to others, people use the respectful ivaru.

The same family words are used to address strangers politely: anna or akka to someone a little older than you, amma to an older woman, taata or ajji to the elderly.

examples.english: My grandfather lives in the village.
My younger brother goes to college.

guide.title: Talking about your family
guide.text:
'I have a brother' uses the dative pattern: nanage + relative + form of iru. Count people with the human number words: obba anna (one elder brother), obbalu tangi (one younger sister), ibbaru makkalu (two children), mooru jana (three people).

'Family' in the sense of household is usually expressed with ಮನೆ (mane), 'house': nimma maneyalli eshtu jana iddaare? 'how many people are there in your house?'. The formal word is ಕುಟುಂಬ (kutumba).

Marriage 'happens to you': ಮದುವೆ ಆಗಿದೆ (maduve aagide) 'is married', literally 'marriage has happened'; ಮದುವೆ ಆಗಿಲ್ಲ (maduve aagilla) 'is not married'. These are everyday questions in India and are not considered intrusive.

phrases.note: ivaru is the respectful word for 'this person'.
Younger brother: tamma (ತಮ್ಮ). anna here has the retroflex ಣ್ಣ.
Elder sister: akka (ಅಕ್ಕ).
'I am married': nanage maduve aagide.
For counting people use 'ibbaru' (two persons), not 'eradu'.

phrases.english: How many people are there in your family?
phrases.note: Literally 'in your house' - the usual way to ask about family.

phrases.english: My grandfather lives in the village.
phrases.note: 'taata' is usual around Bengaluru; elsewhere in Karnataka you will hear 'ajja' (ಅಜ್ಜ).
ellaroo = everyone. A polite question after greeting someone.
For 'husband': ivaru nanna ganda (ಇವರು ನನ್ನ ಗಂಡ).

phrases.english: My elder sister lives in Mysuru.
phrases.note: Plural verb out of respect for an elder.

phrases.english: My younger brother goes to college.
phrases.note: Singular verb for someone younger.

phrases.native: ನಮ್ಮ ಅಜ್ಜಿ ತುಂಬಾ ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿ ಅಡುಗೆ ಮಾಡ್ತಾರೆ.
phrases.roman: namma ajji tumbaa chennaagi aduge maadtaare.
phrases.literal: our grandmother very well cooking does
phrases.note: namma ('our') is the natural word for one's own family members.

units.title: Time, days and dates
units.description: Tell the time, name the days, and talk about yesterday, today, tomorrow, last week and next week.

guide.title: Clock time
guide.text:
ಗಂಟೆ (gante) means 'hour', 'o'clock' and 'bell'. 'What time is it?' is gante eshtaaytu? - literally 'how much has the hour become?'. The answer puts the number first: aidu gante aaytu, or just aidu gante, 'five o'clock'.

'At five o'clock' adds the dative: ಐದು ಗಂಟೆಗೆ (aidu gantege). 'At what time?' is ಎಷ್ಟು ಗಂಟೆಗೆ? (eshtu gantege?).

Half past is the number + -ವರೆ (-vare), with the final u of the number lengthened: ಐದೂವರೆ (aidoovare) half past five; ಏಳೂವರೆ (eloovare) half past seven; ಹತ್ತೂವರೆ (hattoovare) half past ten. Quarter past is the number + ಕಾಲು (kaalu): aidookaalu, 5:15. Quarter to the next hour is said as 'five and three quarters': aidoomukkaalu, 5:45.

Minutes are ನಿಮಿಷ (nimisha): aidu gante hattu nimisha, 5:10. People also read times in English.

Parts of the day: ಬೆಳಿಗ್ಗೆ (beligge) morning; ಮಧ್ಯಾಹ್ನ (madhyaahna) afternoon; ಸಂಜೆ (sanje) evening; ರಾತ್ರಿ (raatri) night. They are used without any ending: sanje barteeni, 'I'll come in the evening'.

guide.title: Days of the week
guide.text:
The days end in ವಾರ (vaara), which on its own means 'week' and also 'day of the week':

ಭಾನುವಾರ (bhaanuvaara) Sunday; ಸೋಮವಾರ (somavaara) Monday; ಮಂಗಳವಾರ (mangalavaara) Tuesday; ಬುಧವಾರ (budhavaara) Wednesday; ಗುರುವಾರ (guruvaara) Thursday; ಶುಕ್ರವಾರ (shukravaara) Friday; ಶನಿವಾರ (shanivaara) Saturday.

'On Monday' needs no ending, or takes -a dina ('day of'): somavaara barteeni, 'I'll come on Monday'.

To ask the day: ivattu yaava vaara? - 'today (is) which weekday?'

guide.title: Yesterday, today, tomorrow
guide.text:
ಮೊನ್ನೆ (monne) the day before yesterday; ನಿನ್ನೆ (ninne) yesterday; ಇವತ್ತು (ivattu) today; ನಾಳೆ (naale) tomorrow; ನಾಡಿದ್ದು (naadiddu) the day after tomorrow.

ivattu is the spoken word; in writing 'today' is ಇಂದು (indu) or ಈ ದಿನ (ee dina).

ಈಗ (eega) now; ಆಮೇಲೆ (aamele) later; ಆಗಲೇ (aagale) already; ಇನ್ನೂ (innoo) still, yet; ಬೇಗ (bega) early, soon; ತಡ (tada) late - though most people say 'let': let aaytu, 'it got late'.

The tense of the verb must match: ninne bande (I came yesterday), naale barteeni (I'll come tomorrow).

examples.english: The day after tomorrow is a holiday.

guide.title: Weeks, months, years and dates
guide.text:
ದಿನ (dina) day; ವಾರ (vaara) week; ತಿಂಗಳು (tingalu) month; ವರ್ಷ (varsha) year.

'Last' is ಹೋದ (hoda, 'that went') or ಕಳೆದ (kaleda); 'next' is ಮುಂದಿನ (mundina) or ಬರೋ (baro, 'that is coming'); 'this' is ಈ (ee): hoda vaara (last week), ee vaara (this week), mundina vaara (next week), hoda varsha (last year), mundina tingalu (next month).

A length of time takes no ending: eradu dina (for two days), mooru varsha (for three years). 'Ago' is ಹಿಂದೆ (hinde, 'behind') after the possessive form of the time: eradu dinada hinde, 'two days ago'. 'In / after two days' is eradu dinadalli or eradu dina aada mele.

For calendar dates, everyday Kannada uses the English month names with ತಾರೀಖು (taareekhu), 'date': aidane taareekhu, 'the fifth'. Ordinals add -ane to the number: ondane (first), eradane (second), moorane (third), aidane (fifth). 'First' is also ಮೊದಲನೇ (modalane).

phrases.note: 'taim eshtaaytu?' (ಟೈಮ್ ಎಷ್ಟಾಯ್ತು?) is just as common.
gantege = at ... o'clock.
elu + vare; the first e is long.
The o of soma is long.

phrases.english: What day of the week is it today?

phrases.note: Spoken form; in writing it is baruttene (ಬರುತ್ತೇನೆ).

phrases.english: The day after tomorrow is a holiday.
phrases.note: raje = holiday, leave.

phrases.english: Last week I was in my home town.
phrases.note: hoda = 'that went', i.e. last.
Literally 'stay for a minute'.
Many speakers say 'let aagtide' (ಲೇಟ್ ಆಗ್ತಿದೆ).
horadu = to set out. Written: horaduttade (ಹೊರಡುತ್ತದೆ).

phrases.english: I don't have time right now.

units.title: Weather and seasons
units.description: Talk about rain, sun, heat and cold, and say how the weather makes you feel.

guide.title: Weather is a noun that comes or is there
guide.text:
English says 'it is raining'. Kannada has no 'it' here: the weather itself is the subject. Rain 'comes'; sun, cold, heat and cloud 'are there'.

ಮಳೆ (male) rain: male barutte (rain comes = it rains), male bartide (it is raining), male bantu (it rained), male nintide (the rain has stopped).
ಬಿಸಿಲು (bisilu) sunshine, heat of the sun: bisilu ide, 'it is sunny'.
ಚಳಿ (chali) cold: chali ide, 'it is cold'.
ಸೆಕೆ (seke) heat, sultriness: seke ide, 'it is hot'.
ಗಾಳಿ (gaali) wind, air: gaali beesutte, 'the wind blows'.
ಮೋಡ (moda) cloud: moda ide, 'it is cloudy'.
ಮಂಜು (manju) mist, fog, dew.

For what the weather is generally like in a place or season, use irutte ('is, as a rule') instead of ide: besigeyalli seke irutte, 'it is hot in summer'.

guide.title: Feeling hot and cold
guide.text:
How the weather feels to you uses the dative pattern with aagu, 'happen': ನನಗೆ ಚಳಿ ಆಗ್ತಿದೆ (nanage chali aagtide), 'cold is happening to me' = 'I am feeling cold'; nanage seke aagtide, 'I am feeling hot'.

Do not say naanu chali or naanu bisi for 'I am cold / hot'.

ಬಿಸಿ (bisi) 'hot' and ತಣ್ಣಗೆ (tannage) 'cold' describe things you touch or eat - coffee, water, food - not the weather. ತಂಪು (tampu) is 'pleasantly cool': tampaagide, 'it is nice and cool'.

ಹವಾಮಾನ (havaamaana) and ವಾತಾವರಣ (vaataavarana) both mean 'weather, climate'; many people simply say 'vedar'.

guide.title: Seasons
guide.text:
Karnataka has three main seasons, each named with ಕಾಲ (kaala), 'time, season':

ಬೇಸಿಗೆ (besige) or ಬೇಸಿಗೆ ಕಾಲ, summer - roughly March to May.
ಮಳೆಗಾಲ (malegaala), the rainy season or monsoon - June to September or October.
ಚಳಿಗಾಲ (chaligaala), winter - November to February.

(kaala becomes -gaala when joined to male and chali.)

'In summer' takes the locative: besigeyalli; malegaaladalli; chaligaaladalli.

Bengaluru is known for its mild weather, and remarking on it is a safe way to start any conversation.

examples.english: It is very hot in summer.
In winter there is mist in the morning.

phrases.note: bisilu is the heat and light of the sun.
male has the retroflex ಳ.
Written: aaguttide (ಆಗುತ್ತಿದೆ).
joraagi = strongly, loudly, fast.
nintu (having stopped) + ide.
Another word for umbrella is kode (ಕೊಡೆ).

phrases.english: The weather in Bengaluru is nice.
It is very hot in summer.
phrases.note: irutte for what is generally true. Written: iruttade (ಇರುತ್ತದೆ).
shuru aagu = to begin.

phrases.english: In winter there is mist in the morning.

phrases.note: The o of moda is long.
barutte + -aa.
tampu (coolness) + aagide.

units.title: Health and emergencies
units.description: Say what is wrong, describe pain and illness, and get help when something goes wrong.

guide.title: Illness comes to you
guide.text:
Illnesses and symptoms use the dative pattern: the sick person is in the dative, and the illness 'has come', 'is there' or 'is happening'.

nanage jvara bandide, 'fever has come to me' = 'I have a fever'.
nanage negadi aagide, 'I have a cold'.
nanage kemmu ide, 'I have a cough'.
nanage vaanti aagtide, 'I am vomiting'.

Words: ಜ್ವರ (jvara) fever; ನೆಗಡಿ (negadi) a cold; ಕೆಮ್ಮು (kemmu) cough; ವಾಂತಿ (vaanti) vomiting; ಭೇದಿ (bhedi) diarrhoea; ಗಾಯ (gaaya) wound, injury; ಅಲರ್ಜಿ (alarji) allergy.

The general 'I'm not well' is ನನಗೆ ಹುಷಾರಿಲ್ಲ (nanage hushaarilla); hushaaru means 'well, alert'. To wish someone well, say hushaaru! - 'take care!'.

guide.title: Pain and parts of the body
guide.text:
ನೋವು (novu, long o) is 'pain'. Put the body part in front: tale novu or talenovu (headache), hotte novu (stomach ache), hallu novu (toothache), bennu novu (backache), gantalu novu (sore throat).

Body parts: ತಲೆ (tale) head; ಕಣ್ಣು (kannu) eye; ಕಿವಿ (kivi) ear; ಮೂಗು (moogu) nose; ಬಾಯಿ (baayi) mouth; ಹಲ್ಲು (hallu) tooth; ಗಂಟಲು (gantalu) throat; ಕೈ (kai) hand, arm; ಕಾಲು (kaalu) leg, foot; ಹೊಟ್ಟೆ (hotte) stomach; ಬೆನ್ನು (bennu) back; ಎದೆ (ede) chest.

'It hurts here' is illi novaagtide (novu + aagtide, 'pain is happening'). 'It hurts a lot' is tumbaa novaagtide.

guide.title: Calling for help
guide.text:
ಸಹಾಯ (sahaaya) is 'help': nanage sahaaya maadi, 'please help me'. In real danger shout ಕಾಪಾಡಿ! (kaapaadi!), 'save me!', or ಬನ್ನಿ! (banni!), 'come!'.

'Call X' is X-annu kareyiri, with the object ending because it is a person: daaktarannu kareyiri, poleesarannu kareyiri. For a vehicle or thing no ending is needed: aambyulens kareyiri.

Losing something: kaleduhogide, 'has got lost'. Theft: kallatana aagide, 'a theft has happened'; ಕಳ್ಳ (kalla) is 'thief'.

ಬೆಂಕಿ (benki) fire; ಅಪಘಾತ (apaghaata) accident - though everyone says 'aaksident'; ಆಸ್ಪತ್ರೆ (aaspatre) hospital; ಪೊಲೀಸ್ ಸ್ಟೇಷನ್ (polees steshan) police station.

guide.title: At the doctor's and the pharmacy
guide.text:
ಔಷಧಿ (aushadhi) is 'medicine'; a tablet is ಮಾತ್ರೆ (maatre). A pharmacy is aushadhi angadi, but everyone says 'medikal shaap' or just 'medikals'.

Instructions you will hear: ದಿನಕ್ಕೆ ಎರಡು ಸಲ (dinakke eradu sala) twice a day - sala means 'time, occasion'; ಊಟ ಆದ ಮೇಲೆ (oota aada mele) after food; ಊಟಕ್ಕೆ ಮುಂಚೆ (ootakke munche) before food; ಮೂರು ದಿನ (mooru dina) for three days.

The doctor may ask: enaagide? 'what has happened?'; yaavaaginda? 'since when?'; elli novu? 'where is the pain?'. To answer 'since yesterday': ninneyinda; 'for two days': eradu dinadinda.

examples.english: I have had a fever for two days.

phrases.note: To shout for help, cry 'kaapaadi!' (ಕಾಪಾಡಿ!).
polees + the plural -aru + the object ending -annu.
The Kannada word for doctor is vaidya (ವೈದ್ಯ), used in writing.
The ambulance number in India is 108.
A very common everyday expression in Bengaluru.
In practice people ask for the 'medical shop': medikal shaap ellide?
Literally 'my phone has got lost'.
Literally 'fever has come to me'.
The o of hotte is short; the o of novu is long.
Point to the place while saying it.

units.title: Phone and appointments
units.description: Make and answer phone calls, ask for someone, and fix a time to meet.

guide.title: On the phone
guide.text:
'To phone' is fon maadu, literally 'do phone'; many people also say kaal maadu. 'To message' is mesej maadu. The person you call is in the dative: nimage fon maadteeni, 'I'll call you'.

A call begins with ಹಲೋ (halo). To ask who is calling: yaaru maataadtirodu? - 'who (is it that is) speaking?'. maataadtirodu is the spoken verbal noun 'the one speaking'; the written form is ಮಾತಾಡುತ್ತಿರುವುದು (maataaduttiruvudu).

To say who you are: naanu ravi maataadtiddeeni, 'I Ravi am-speaking'.

When the line is bad: ಕೇಳಿಸ್ತಿಲ್ಲ (kelistilla), 'it is not audible' = 'I can't hear you'; svalpa joraagi maataadi, 'speak a little louder'. kelisu means 'to be heard'; kelistide is 'I can hear you'.

To end a call people say fon idteeni, 'I'll put the phone down', or simply sari, sigona.

guide.title: Asking for someone
guide.text:
To ask whether someone is there, use the respectful plural of iru with the question ending: ravi iddaaraa? 'Is Ravi there?'. Adding ಅವರು (avaru) after a name is the polite equivalent of Mr or Ms: ravi avaru iddaaraa?

Possible answers: iddaare, 'yes, he is'; avaru eega illa, 'he is not here now'; horage hogiddaare, 'he has gone out'; ondu nimisha, 'one moment'.

To leave word: naanu fon maadidde anta heli, 'please say that I called' (anta marks what is to be said - see the unit on joining sentences).

guide.title: Fixing a time
guide.text:
ಸಿಗು (sigu) means 'to be found, to be got' and is the everyday verb for 'meet': sigona, 'let's meet'; naale sigteeni, 'I'll see you tomorrow'.

To ask whether something is possible, use the -oke form + aaguttaa?: naale sigoke aaguttaa? 'is it possible to meet tomorrow?'. Answers: aagutte, 'yes, that works'; aagalla, 'no, I can't'.

Time expressions: eshtu gantege? 'at what time?'; hattu gantege, 'at ten'; sanje aidu gantege, 'at five in the evening'; naale beligge, 'tomorrow morning'.

'Late' is tada, or far more often the English word: letaagi, 'late (as an adverb)'; let aagutte, 'it will get late'.

Appointments use the English word: apaayintment.

examples.english: Tomorrow isn't possible; the day after is fine.

phrases.note: Written: maataaduttiruvudu (ಮಾತಾಡುತ್ತಿರುವುದು).
Put your own name in place of Ravi.
iddaare + -aa. More formal: ravi avaru iddaaraa?
Literally 'it is not being heard'. Written: kelisuttilla (ಕೇಳಿಸುತ್ತಿಲ್ಲ).
Written: sigalu aaguttadeyaa? (ಸಿಗಲು ಆಗುತ್ತದೆಯಾ?)
letaagi = let + aagi, 'being late'. Pure Kannada: tadavaagi (ತಡವಾಗಿ).
The usual way to close a call.

units.title: Travel and staying somewhere
units.description: Buy tickets, check buses and trains, and take a room in a hotel.

guide.title: Tickets, buses and trains
guide.text:
To buy a ticket, name the destination with the 'to' ending, then the number of tickets: maisoorige ondu tiket kodi, 'one ticket to Mysuru, please'; eradu tiket, 'two tickets'.

To check a bus or train: ee bas maisoorige hoguttaa? 'does this bus go to Mysuru?'. Buses and trains are neuter, so the verbs end in -utte: hogutte (goes), barutte (comes), horadutte (leaves), nillutte (stops).

Getting on and off: ಹತ್ತು (hattu) climb, get on - polite command ಹತ್ತಿ (hatti); ಇಳಿ (ili) get down, get off - polite command ಇಳಿಯಿರಿ (iliyiri). naanu illi iliyabeku, 'I need to get off here'.

ಸೀಟ್ (seet) seat; ಖಾಲಿ (khaali) empty, free; ಮುಂದಿನ ಸ್ಟಾಪ್ (mundina staap) the next stop; ಲಗೇಜ್ (lagej) luggage.

examples.english: Does this bus go to Mysuru?
I need to get off here.

guide.title: How long, how much per day
guide.text:
'How long?' is ಎಷ್ಟು ಹೊತ್ತು? (eshtu hottu?) - hottu means 'a stretch of time'. 'It takes two hours' is eradu gante aagutte, 'two hours happen'.

'Per' is the dative: ondu dinakke eshtu? 'how much for one day?'; talege nooru roopaayi, 'a hundred rupees a head'.

Lengths of stay take no ending: naanu mooru dina irteeni, 'I'll stay three days'; ondu vaara, 'for a week'.

'Until' is ತನಕ (tanaka) or ವರೆಗೆ (varege) after the time: shukravaara tanaka, 'until Friday'.

examples.english: How long does it take to the airport?

guide.title: At a hotel or guest house
guide.text:
ರೂಮ್ (room) is 'room'; the Kannada word ಕೋಣೆ (kone) is used for rooms of a house. room khaali ideyaa? asks whether a room is free. torisi, 'please show', lets you see it first.

Things to ask about use ide / ideyaa or barutte / baruttaa: bisi neeru baruttaa? 'does hot water come?'; vaifai ideyaa? 'is there wifi?'; e.si. ideyaa? 'is there air conditioning?'.

To ask permission use -abahudaa: illi idabahudaa? 'may I keep (it) here?'.

To find out what to see: illi nodoke enenide? 'what all is there to see here?'. enenu ('what all') is enu doubled; enenide is enenu + ide.

examples.english: Do you have a room free?
What is there to see here?

phrases.english: Does this bus go to Mysuru?
phrases.note: hogutte + -aa. Written: hoguttadeyaa? (ಹೋಗುತ್ತದೆಯಾ?)

phrases.english: What time does the train arrive?
phrases.note: The Kannada word for train is railu (ರೈಲು).

phrases.english: I need to get off here.
phrases.note: The l of ili is the retroflex ಳ. Fast speech: ileebeku (ಇಳೀಬೇಕು).

phrases.english: How long does it take to the airport?
Do you have a room free?

phrases.note: The dative gives 'per'.
Water 'comes' from the tap.

phrases.english: May I leave my luggage here?
What is there to see here?
phrases.note: Both e of enen- are long.

units.title: At work or study
units.description: Talk about your job, your studies and the day's work with colleagues and classmates.

guide.title: Work words
guide.text:
ಕೆಲಸ (kelasa) is 'work' and also 'job': kelasa maadu, 'to work'; kelasa ide, 'there is work (to do)'; kelasa sikkitu, '(I) got a job'.

Where you work takes the locative: kampaniyalli (in a company), byaankinalli (in a bank), shaaleyalli (in a school), aaspatreyalli (in a hospital).

Office life borrows heavily from English, with Kannada verbs and endings: meeting ide (there is a meeting), meel kalisi (send a mail), raje haaku (to put in for leave), let aaytu (it got late). ಸಂಬಳ (sambala) is 'salary'; ರಜೆ (raje) is 'leave, holiday'.

ಮುಗಿ (mugi) is 'to come to an end' and ಮುಗಿಸು (mugisu) 'to finish something': kelasa mugiyitu, 'the work ended'; kelasa mugiside, 'I finished the work'. Many Kannada verbs come in such pairs, the second with -isu meaning 'cause it to happen': nillu / nillisu (stop), kali / kalisu (learn / teach).

examples.english: There is a lot of work today.
This work must be finished today itself.

guide.title: Studying
guide.text:
ಓದು (odu, long o) means both 'read' and 'study': enu odtiddeera? 'what are you studying?'; naanu injiniyaring odtiddeeni.

ಕಲಿ (kali) is 'learn': kannada kaleetiddeeni, 'I am learning Kannada'. ಬರೆ (bare) is 'write': bareeteeni, 'I write'; bareyiri, 'please write'.

ಶಾಲೆ (shaale) school; ಕಾಲೇಜು (kaaleju) college; ಪರೀಕ್ಷೆ (pareekshe) exam; ಪಾಠ (paatha) lesson; ವಿದ್ಯಾರ್ಥಿ (vidyaarthi) student; ಶಿಕ್ಷಕ (shikshaka) teacher - though 'teechar' and 'saar / medam' are what students actually say.

Understanding 'happens to you': nanage artha aagutte, 'I understand'; artha aagalilla, 'I didn't understand'; artha aaytaa? 'did you understand?'. artha means 'meaning'.

guide.title: 'Not yet' and 'still going on'
guide.text:
ಇನ್ನೂ (innoo) means 'still' with a positive verb and 'yet' with a negative one.

With the negative perfect (participle + illa) it gives 'has not ... yet': sambala innoo bandilla, 'the salary hasn't come yet'; kelasa innoo mugidilla, 'the work isn't finished yet'; avaru innoo bandilla, 'they haven't come yet'.

With the continuous it gives 'still ...ing': innoo kelasa maadtiddeeni, 'I am still working'.

ಆಗಲೇ (aagale) is 'already': aagale mugiside, 'I have already finished'.

To ask how something is going, use nade, 'walk, go on': kelasa hege nadeetide? 'how is the work going?'. The stock answer is chennaagi nadeetide, 'it is going well'.

phrases.english: I work at a software company.
My office is right near here.
There is a lot of work today.

phrases.note: raje haaku = to apply for leave.

phrases.english: This work must be finished today itself.
phrases.note: ivattu + emphatic -e; the final e is long.
Could also mean 'What are you reading?'
vivarisu = to explain.
Written: nadeyuttide (ನಡೆಯುತ್ತಿದೆ).
bandu + illa.

units.title: Everyday conversation
units.description: Keep a simple conversation going: say when you do not understand, ask what words mean and make small talk.

guide.title: When you don't understand
guide.text:
These are the phrases that let you stay in Kannada instead of switching to English.

nanage artha aagtilla, 'I am not understanding' - artha is 'meaning', and understanding 'happens to you'. If you did not catch something already said: artha aagalilla, 'I didn't understand'.

svalpa nidhaanavaagi maataadi, 'please speak a little slowly'. innondu sala heli, 'say it one more time' - innondu is innu ('more') + ondu ('one'), and sala is 'time, occasion'.

To ask about words: idara artha enu? 'what is the meaning of this?'; idakke enantaare? 'what do they call this?'; idakke kannadadalli enantaare? 'what is this called in Kannada?'.

nanage gottilla, 'I don't know'; nanage gottu, 'I know'.

examples.english: What is this called in Kannada?

guide.title: Languages 'come to you'
guide.text:
To say you know a language, Kannada says it 'comes' to you: nanage kannada barutte, 'Kannada comes to me' = 'I know / speak Kannada'. The question is nimage inglish baruttaa? and the negative nanage baralla.

svalpa svalpa, 'a little little', is the modest and charming answer every learner should have ready: nanage svalpa svalpa kannada barutte.

You can also use gottu, 'known': nimage kannada gottaa? 'do you know Kannada?'.

When people hear you try, they will very likely say neevu kannada chennaagi maataadteera, 'you speak Kannada well'. A good reply is illa, innoo kaleetiddeeni - 'no, I am still learning'.

guide.title: Small talk
guide.text:
Conversations between acquaintances open with a few fixed moves.

ಮತ್ತೆ? (matte?) literally 'again, and then?' is the universal prompt: 'so, what else?'. matte, enu samaachaara? is 'so, what's the news?'. The standard answer is enoo illa, 'nothing', followed by ellaa aaraama, 'all is well'.

ಆರಾಮ (aaraama) means 'comfortable, well': aaraamaa? 'are you well?' - aaraama. In north Karnataka this is the normal 'how are you'.

Safe topics: the weather (ivattu tumbaa seke ide), food (oota aaytaa?), where you are from (nimma ooru yaavudu?), and how you like the place (nanage ee jaaga tumbaa ishta).

paravaagilla - 'it doesn't matter, no problem' - answers both apologies and thanks, and also means 'not bad'.

phrases.note: Written: aaguttilla (ಆಗುತ್ತಿಲ್ಲ).
'svalpa' (a little) softens the request, like 'please'.
Literally 'Does English come to you?'
Written: baruttade (ಬರುತ್ತದೆ). Also pronounced baratte.

Also the usual reply to 'sorry' or 'thank you'.
A compliment you will hear often.
The classic small-talk opener.

units.title: Feelings and opinions
units.description: Say how you feel, what you like and what you think, and agree or disagree politely.

guide.title: Feelings happen to you
guide.text:
In Kannada you do not 'be' happy or tired; the feeling happens or comes to you. The person is in the dative, the feeling is a noun, and the verb is a form of aagu ('happen') or baa ('come').

ಖುಷಿ (khushi) happiness, ಸಂತೋಷ (santosha) joy: nanage khushi aaytu, 'I became happy, I am glad'.
ಬೇಜಾರು (bejaaru) boredom, low spirits, being upset: nanage bejaaraagide.
ಸುಸ್ತು (sustu) tiredness: nanage sustaagide, 'I am tired'.
ಭಯ (bhaya) fear: nanage bhaya aagtide, 'I am scared'.
ಕೋಪ (kopa) anger: nanage kopa bandide, 'anger has come to me' = 'I am angry'.
ನಿದ್ದೆ (nidde) sleep: nanage nidde bartide, 'I am sleepy'.
ಆಶ್ಚರ್ಯ (aashcharya) surprise: nanage aashcharya aaytu, 'I was surprised'.

The tense tells the story: aaytu (it happened - a reaction to news), aagide (it has happened - the state now), aagtide (it is happening - building up right now).

examples.english: I am very happy (to hear or see that).

guide.title: Likes and dislikes
guide.text:
ಇಷ್ಟ (ishta) is 'liking': nanage ee haadu ishta, 'I like this song'. tumbaa ishta is 'like very much'.

For a reaction to something you have just tried, use ishta aaytu, 'liking happened' = 'I liked it', and ishta aagalilla, 'I didn't like it'.

Praise: chennaagide (it is good/nice); tumbaa chennaagide (very nice); sooper! - the English word, used constantly.

Sympathy and dismay: ಪಾಪ (paapa) 'poor thing!'; ಅಯ್ಯೋ (ayyo) 'oh no!'; ಛೆ (chhe) 'tut, what a shame'.

guide.title: Giving an opinion
guide.text:
'I think that ...' is built with ಅಂತ (anta), which closes off the thought like a spoken quotation mark, followed by nanage annisutte, 'it seems to me': idu sari anta nanage annisutte, 'this is right - so it seems to me' = 'I think this is right'. Negative: annisalla; nanage haage annisalla, 'I don't think so'.

The thought comes first and 'I think' comes last - the reverse of English.

Other ways to give a view: ನನ್ನ ಪ್ರಕಾರ (nanna prakaara) 'according to me, in my view'; ಇರಬಹುದು (irabahudu) 'maybe, could be'.

Agreeing: ಸರಿ (sari) right; neevu heliddu sari, 'what you said is right' (heliddu = 'that which was said'); haudu, nija, 'yes, true'.

Disagreeing politely: haage alla, 'it is not like that'; nanage haage annisalla. To ask: nimma abhipraaya enu? 'what is your opinion?' or simply nimage enu annisutte? 'what do you think?'

phrases.english: I am very happy about that.
phrases.note: A reaction to good news. More formal: santosha aaytu.
bejaaru covers bored, fed up, sad and upset.
sustu + aagide.
The o of kopa is long.
Written: annisuvudilla (ಅನ್ನಿಸುವುದಿಲ್ಲ).
anta marks the end of the thought. Written: endu (ಎಂದು) ... annisuttade (ಅನ್ನಿಸುತ್ತದೆ).
Literally 'what you said is right'.
Less formal: nimage enu annisutte?
Said in sympathy.
A warm response to good news or to a thank-you.

units.title: Joining sentences
units.description: Connect ideas with and, but, or, because, so, if, when, before, after and 'that'.

guide.title: And, also, but, or
guide.text:
ಮತ್ತು (mattu) is 'and' between nouns: tee mattu kaafi. In speech it is often left out, or replaced by adding a long -oo to each item: ನಾನೂ ನೀವೂ (naanoo neevoo), 'both I and you'.

On a single word -oo means 'also, too': naanoo barteeni, 'I too will come'; idoo beku, 'I want this as well'.

To join two actions, Kannada does not use 'and' at all - it uses the 'having done' form: oota maadi banni, 'eat and come'.

ಆದ್ರೆ (aadre) is 'but'; the written form is ಆದರೆ (aadare).

ಅಥವಾ (athavaa) is 'or' in statements and choices. In everyday speech you also hear ಇಲ್ಲಾಂದ್ರೆ (illaandre), 'if not, otherwise'. For 'A or B?' questions remember the -aa ... -aa pattern: tee bekaa, kaafi bekaa?

examples.native: ಬರಬೇಕು ಅಂತ ಇದೆ, ಆದ್ರೆ ಸಮಯ ಇಲ್ಲ.
examples.roman: barabeku anta ide, aadre samaya illa.
examples.english: I'd like to come, but I have no time.

guide.title: Because and so
guide.text:
ಯಾಕಂದ್ರೆ (yaakandre), 'because', is literally 'if you say why'. It comes at the start of the reason, after the main statement, just as in English: naanu baralla, yaakandre kelasa ide. The written form is ಏಕೆಂದರೆ (ekendare).

More natural in Kannada is to give the reason first and then say ಅದಕ್ಕೆ (adakke), 'for that, so, that's why': nanage hushaarilla, adakke baralilla, 'I am unwell, that's why I didn't come'.

A reason can also be attached to a noun with -inda: maleyinda, 'because of the rain'.

examples.english: I won't come, because I have work.
I am unwell, so I didn't come.
I got late because of the rain.

guide.title: If
guide.text:
'If' is not a separate word but an ending on the verb: past stem + -ರೆ (-re). In speech: bandre (if ... come), hodre (if ... go), maadidre (if ... do), nodidre (if ... see), kotre (if ... give), idre (if ... is), aadre (if ... becomes - this is where 'but' comes from). Written forms keep an a: bandare, hodare, maadidare, iddare.

The form is the same for every person; the subject is shown by a pronoun: neevu bandre, 'if you come'; male bandre, 'if it rains'.

The 'if' clause comes first. For 'it would be good if ...' finish with chennaagirutte.

Negative 'if not': negative participle + idre: barade idre (ಬರದೆ ಇದ್ರೆ), 'if (you) don't come'. With nouns and adjectives use illaandre / illa andre, 'if not'.

gottidre (gottu + idre) is 'if (you) know'; bekaadre (beku + aadre) is 'if (you) want'; saadhya aadre, 'if possible'.

examples.english: If it rains, I won't come.
It would be nice if you came.

guide.title: When, after, before, until
guide.text:
These too are endings or words placed after a verb form - the time clause always comes first.

When: past stem + -ಆಗ (-aaga): bandaaga (when ... came / comes), hodaaga (when ... went), iddaaga (when ... was), nodidaaga (when ... saw). neevu bandaaga fon maadi, 'call when you come'.

After: past stem + -a + ಮೇಲೆ (mele): banda mele (after coming), hoda mele (after going), oota aada mele (after the meal is over).

Before: the -oke form (or the written -uva form) + ಮುಂಚೆ (munche): hogoke munche, 'before going'; oota maadoke munche, 'before eating'. With a noun, use the dative: ootakke munche, 'before the meal'.

Until: the spoken relative participle ('that comes' form) in -o + ತನಕ (tanaka): naanu baro tanaka, 'until I come'. baro is the spoken form of baruva, 'that comes'.

examples.english: Stay right here until I come.

guide.title: 'That': the quoting word anta
guide.text:
ಅಂತ (anta) is placed after anything said, thought, heard or known, and works like 'that' or like closing quotation marks. The quoted words come first and keep the form the original speaker used:

avaru 'naale barteeni' anta helidru - literally 'he "tomorrow I-will-come" thus said' = 'he said he would come tomorrow'. Notice that the verb inside stays barteeni ('I will come'), exactly as he said it.

It is used with heli (say), keli (ask), gottu (know), annisutte (seems), andkonde ('I thought'): avaru bartaare anta gottu, 'I know that they are coming'.

anta + ide after -beku expresses a wish: hogabeku anta ide, 'I feel like going'.

The written form of anta is ಎಂದು (endu).

examples.english: He said he would come tomorrow.
I know that they are coming.

phrases.note: mattu joins nouns, not actions.
naanu + -oo.

units.title: Three complete dialogues
units.description: Follow and take part in three real-life exchanges: meeting a neighbour, ordering at an eatery and taking an auto.

guide.title: How to use this unit
guide.text:
Each of the next three sections is a short conversation between two people, A and B, given line by line. Nothing in them is new grammar: every form has been taught in an earlier unit. Read each dialogue aloud several times, first as A and then as B, until you can say your lines without looking.

Things to notice as you read: the verb is always last; subjects are dropped when the verb ending makes them clear; yes/no questions end in a long -aa; and requests end in the polite -i.

The practice phrases below are the same lines, so the quiz will test whether you really understood each one.

guide.title: Dialogue 1: Meeting a neighbour
guide.text:
A is a long-time resident; B has just moved in. A opens with a guess ('are you new here?'), which is friendlier than a direct 'who are you?'. hosabaru is 'a new person' (from hosa, 'new'), in the respectful plural, and -aa makes it a question.

B answers with the past tense bande ('I came') and no pronoun. ooru is one's home town. In the last two lines A pays the standard compliment, and B gives the standard modest reply with the continuous form kaleetiddeeni, 'I am learning'.

Lines: A, B, A, B, A, B.

examples.english: A: Hello, are you new here?
B: Yes, I came last week.
A: Which is your home town?

guide.title: Dialogue 2: At a small eatery
guide.text:
A is the person at the counter of a darshini, the stand-up eateries found all over Bengaluru; B is the customer.

enu kodali? is 'what shall I give?' - the -ali form used with a question word. B orders with numbers and kodi. kudiyoke is the -oke form of kudi: 'to drink, for drinking'. In A's last line, two questions with -aa give the either/or choice: 'will you eat right here, or will you take it away?'. B answers with tinteeni and then asks the bill with eshtaaytu?, 'how much did it come to?'.

Lines: A, B, A, B, A, B.

examples.english: A: What can I get you?
B: Two idlis and one vada, please.
A: What would you like to drink?
A: Will you eat here or take it away?
B: I'll eat here. How much is it?

guide.title: Dialogue 3: Taking an auto
guide.text:
A is the passenger, B the auto-rickshaw driver. A names the place with the 'to' ending (-kke after a name ending in -a) and asks barteeraa?, 'will you come?'. B agrees with the same verb in the 'I' form: barteeni.

eshtu aagutte? is 'how much will it be?'. meetar mele ippattu is 'twenty on top of the meter' - a common demand; mele is 'on, above'.

The last two lines are A's instructions during the ride: svalpa bega softens 'go fast', and ille edagade is 'right here, on the left side'.

Lines: A, B, A, B, A, A.

examples.english: A: Auto! Will you go to Jayanagar?
A: How much will it be?
A: All right, please go a bit fast.
A: Stop right here on the left.
